note: Shares of world production are rounded, curated figures meant to show proportion. What is live on this page is the alert state: each morning's news is matched against these commodities and routes, so a disruption shows up the day it is reported.

crude_oil.name: Crude oil
crude_oil.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
crude_oil.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

natural_gas.name: Natural gas & LNG
natural_gas.everyday: Cooking gas cylinders, piped kitchen gas, electricity, and urea fertiliser — which is made from gas
natural_gas.india: About half of India's gas is imported as LNG. Expensive gas raises both the power bill and the fertiliser subsidy the government pays.

rice.name: Rice
rice.everyday: The staple on half the world's plates
rice.india: India is the largest exporter, so here the risk runs the other way: when India restricts exports to protect its own prices, the shortage lands on buyers in Africa and Asia.

wheat.name: Wheat
wheat.india: India mostly grows its own, but world prices still set the floor under domestic wheat and feed into bread and biscuit costs.

palm_oil.name: Palm oil
palm_oil.everyday: The cheapest cooking oil, plus soap, biscuits, chocolate, instant noodles and cosmetics
palm_oil.india: India is the world's biggest buyer of edible oils and imports roughly 60% of what it uses, most of it palm. A palm oil shock reaches an Indian kitchen within weeks.

sugar.name: Sugar
sugar.everyday: Sweets, soft drinks, biscuits, and — through ethanol — a slice of your petrol
sugar.india: India is both a huge producer and a swing exporter. Policy here moves the world price, and the world price moves Indian sugar company profits.

fertiliser.name: Fertiliser
fertiliser.everyday: Not bought by you — but it decides how much food a farmer can grow, so it sets the price of all of it a season later
fertiliser.india: India imports most of its potash and much of its urea. Costly fertiliser becomes either a bigger government subsidy or a smaller harvest, and usually both.

copper.name: Copper
copper.everyday: Every wire in your home, every motor, every charger, the electricity grid itself
copper.india: India imports copper concentrate. It is also the metal the whole electrification push runs on, so this is a long-term structural dependence, not a passing one.

iron_ore.name: Iron ore & steel
iron_ore.everyday: Buildings, cars, bridges, railways, the cost of construction
iron_ore.india: India has its own iron ore and is a major steel producer, so here India is a competitor rather than a dependent — world steel prices set Indian steel company profits.

lithium.name: Lithium
lithium.everyday: Phone batteries, laptop batteries, electric scooters and cars, grid storage
lithium.india: India imports essentially all of it. Every electric vehicle sold in India contains someone else's lithium.

cobalt.name: Cobalt
cobalt.everyday: Battery cathodes — the part that decides how long a charge lasts
cobalt.india: Entirely imported, and the supply is more concentrated in one country than almost anything else on this page.

rare_earths.name: Rare earth magnets
rare_earths.everyday: Earphones, phone speakers, electric motors, wind turbines, hard drives, defence equipment
rare_earths.india: India has deposits but almost no processing. The bottleneck is not the rock — it is who can refine it, and that is overwhelmingly one country.

semiconductors.name: Advanced chips
semiconductors.everyday: Phones, cars, appliances, ATMs, UPI itself — a modern car has over a thousand
semiconductors.india: India designs a lot of chips and manufactures almost none of the advanced ones yet. The 2021 chip shortage left Indian car buyers waiting months.

coffee.name: Coffee
coffee.everyday: Your cup, and the price on every café menu
coffee.india: India grows and exports coffee, so a Brazilian frost is good news for Indian growers and bad news for Indian drinkers.

cocoa.name: Cocoa
cocoa.everyday: Chocolate, and anything with chocolate in it
cocoa.india: Almost entirely imported. The 2024 cocoa price spike is the reason chocolate bars quietly shrank.

gold.name: Gold
gold.everyday: Jewellery, weddings, and the thing Indian households save in when they trust nothing else
gold.india: India is the second largest consumer in the world and produces almost none of it. Gold imports are the second biggest item on the import bill after oil.

shipping.name: Container shipping
shipping.everyday: The freight cost buried inside the price of every imported thing you own
shipping.india: Roughly 95% of India's trade by volume moves by sea. Freight rates are a tax on everything, paid invisibly.

soybeans.name: Soybeans & soy oil
soybeans.everyday: Cooking oil, and — as animal feed — the real cost behind chicken, eggs and milk
soybeans.india: India imports soy oil as part of its edible oil basket, and soymeal prices feed straight into Indian poultry and dairy costs.

corn.name: Corn (maize)
corn.everyday: Animal feed first, then starch, sweeteners and ethanol — most of it is eaten by livestock, not people
corn.india: India grows most of what it uses, but world corn prices set the cost of poultry feed, which is why chicken prices track a crop grown in Iowa.

natural_rubber.name: Natural rubber
natural_rubber.everyday: Tyres above all — a truck tyre needs natural rubber that synthetic cannot replace — plus gloves, footwear and seals
natural_rubber.india: India is a major tyre manufacturer and a net importer of rubber. Kerala grows some, nowhere near enough.

tea.name: Tea
tea.everyday: The most-drunk prepared beverage on earth after water
tea.india: India is both a top-two producer and a huge consumer. Domestic prices are set mostly at home, so this is an export-earnings story rather than an inflation one.

spices.name: Spices
spices.everyday: Chilli, turmeric, cumin, pepper, cardamom — the base of most of the world's cooking
spices.india: India dominates this more completely than it dominates anything else. Here India IS the supply risk for everyone else.

cotton.name: Cotton
cotton.everyday: Clothing, bedsheets, towels — roughly a quarter of the world's fibre
cotton.india: India is a top producer and the backbone of its textile industry, which is one of the country's largest employers after agriculture.

onion.name: Onions
onion.everyday: Unremarkable everywhere else; politically explosive in India
onion.india: Onion prices have contributed to governments losing elections in India. No other vegetable carries this much political weight.

nickel.name: Nickel
nickel.everyday: Stainless steel — sinks, cutlery, utensils — and the cathode in longer-range electric vehicle batteries
nickel.india: Almost entirely imported, for both stainless steel manufacturing and the battery supply chain India is trying to build.

aluminium.name: Aluminium & bauxite
aluminium.everyday: Cans, foil, window frames, aircraft, electricity cables, and increasingly car bodies
aluminium.india: India has bauxite and significant smelting capacity, so it is a competitor here — but smelting is enormously power-hungry, which ties it to coal prices.

graphite.name: Graphite
graphite.everyday: The anode in every lithium-ion battery — the half of the battery nobody talks about
graphite.india: Imported. There is more graphite than lithium in a battery by weight, and the supply is more concentrated.

uranium.name: Uranium
uranium.everyday: Nuclear electricity — about a tenth of the world's power, and rising as countries look for clean baseload
uranium.india: India imports uranium for its civil reactors under international agreements, and nuclear is central to its clean-power plans.

phosphate.name: Phosphate rock
phosphate.everyday: The P in NPK fertiliser. There is no substitute — plants need phosphorus and it cannot be manufactured
phosphate.india: India imports nearly all of it. One of the least-known and most absolute dependencies on this page.

potash.name: Potash
potash.everyday: The K in NPK fertiliser, which is what makes crops resilient and improves yields
potash.india: India imports 100% of its potash. There are no commercially viable deposits in the country at all.

palladium.name: Palladium & platinum
palladium.everyday: Catalytic converters that clean car exhaust; platinum also goes into hydrogen equipment
palladium.india: Car manufacturing input costs, and a genuine constraint on meeting tighter emissions standards.

silver.name: Silver
silver.everyday: Jewellery and investment, but more than half of it is industrial now — solar panels above all
silver.india: India is one of the largest silver importers in the world, for both jewellery and a fast-growing solar industry.

coal.name: Coal
coal.everyday: Electricity, and the heat that makes steel and cement
coal.india: India mines a great deal and still imports more, because domestic coal is lower quality. Coal shortages have caused Indian power cuts repeatedly.

chip_equipment.name: Chipmaking machines
chip_equipment.everyday: Nothing you can buy — but no advanced chip exists without these machines, so everything with a chip depends on them
chip_equipment.india: Relevant to India's semiconductor plans: you cannot build a leading-edge fab without machines only a handful of firms make.

pharma_api.name: Medicine ingredients
pharma_api.everyday: The active ingredient inside every tablet you take — paracetamol, antibiotics, blood pressure pills
pharma_api.india: India makes a fifth of the world's generic medicines by volume but imports a large share of the raw ingredients, mostly from China. The pharmacy of the world buys its chemicals from one supplier.

supplies.what: Saudi Arabia is the only producer holding meaningful spare capacity — roughly 2-3 million barrels a day it can switch on within weeks. That spare capacity, not its total output, is what makes it the world's shock absorber. When anyone else fails, Saudi Arabia is the reason the price does not go to the moon.

dependents.detail: Its largest single crude supplier for years
Over half their crude comes from the Gulf
Among the top three suppliers, though India has diversified heavily toward discounted Russian barrels since 2022

risks: OPEC+ production decisions, which are political as much as commercial
Attacks on processing facilities — Abqaiq handles a large share of its output in one place
Regional conflict closing Hormuz, through which most of its exports leave
supplies.if_disrupted: Because this is the world's spare capacity, losing Saudi output is doubly damaging: supply falls AND the cushion that would normally absorb it disappears at the same time. This is the single largest upside risk to the oil price that exists.
supplies.india: Petrol and diesel within weeks, then bus and freight fares, then the rupee as the import bill widens, then inflation, then the RBI's room to cut rates. The chain is short and it has run many times.

history.what: Drone and missile strikes on the Abqaiq processing facility and the Khurais field cut Saudi output by 5.7 million barrels a day overnight — about 5% of world supply, the largest single supply loss in history.
history.why: Attacks attributed to Houthi forces amid the Yemen conflict. The vulnerability was concentration: Abqaiq processes a very large share of Saudi crude in one location.
history.how_long: Oil jumped nearly 15% in a day — the biggest one-day move on record. Saudi Arabia restored output far faster than anyone expected, within about three weeks.
history.response: Emergency drawdown from storage, the IEA signalling readiness to release strategic reserves, and a rapid repair effort. Saudi Arabia afterwards invested heavily in air defence and in spreading processing across more sites.
history.lesson: The world had assumed the risk was a blocked shipping lane. It turned out a few drones hitting one processing plant could do more, faster, and more cheaply. Concentration inside a country matters as much as concentration between countries.

info.name: Crude oil
info.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
info.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

supplies.what: Russia's oil did not leave the market after 2022 — it changed direction. Barrels that went to Europe now go to India and China at a discount, carried by a 'shadow fleet' of older tankers outside Western insurance. The world learned that sanctioning a major producer reroutes oil rather than removing it.

dependents.detail: From under 2% of imports before 2022 to roughly a third — the single biggest change in India's energy sourcing in decades
The largest buyer, much of it by pipeline and therefore immune to shipping risk
A major buyer and a refining re-export hub

risks: Tighter sanctions enforcement on the shadow fleet and its insurers
Price caps being lowered, which narrows the discount India enjoys
Attacks on refineries and export terminals
supplies.if_disrupted: A genuine loss of Russian barrels would be severe, because OPEC+ spare capacity could not fully replace both the volume and the specific grades refiners are configured for. The discount Indian refiners currently enjoy would disappear first, well before any physical shortage.
supplies.india: This is currently a saving, not a risk — discounted Russian crude has measurably reduced India's import bill and helped keep the rupee steadier than it would otherwise have been. The exposure is that the saving can be withdrawn by other countries' policy decisions.

history.what: After the invasion of Ukraine, the G7 imposed a price cap rather than an outright ban, allowing Russian oil to be shipped only if sold below a set price.
history.why: An outright embargo on the world's third largest producer would have sent prices to levels that hurt the sanctioning countries more than the target.
history.how_long: Ongoing, with repeated adjustments.
history.response: The price cap mechanism — a deliberately partial sanction, designed to keep oil flowing while reducing Russian revenue.
history.lesson: When a supplier is too large to remove, policy bends around them. The cap is an admission that the world could not afford to lose the barrels, and India was the main beneficiary of that arithmetic.

info.name: Crude oil
info.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
info.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

supplies.what: Russia and Belarus together dominate potash, and Russian natural gas is the feedstock for much of the world's urea. This is the quiet half of the food security story: you cannot grow food without it, and it is more concentrated than the grain it helps produce.

dependents.detail: Imports the large majority of its fertiliser, and its soy and coffee crops depend on it
Imports most of its potash and a large share of urea
Price-sensitive, and the first to simply use less when costs rise

risks: Sanctions and payment restrictions, even when fertiliser itself is exempt
Expensive natural gas, which raises urea costs everywhere
Export quotas imposed to protect domestic farmers
supplies.if_disrupted: Fertiliser shocks work with a delay of one growing season, which makes them easy to underestimate. Farmers use less, yields fall, and the food price rise arrives six to twelve months later — long after the news has moved on.
supplies.india: Either a bigger subsidy bill for the government or smaller harvests for farmers, and usually some of both. The 2022 spike added heavily to India's fertiliser subsidy.

history.what: Fertiliser prices roughly tripled, driven first by expensive natural gas and then by the Ukraine war and sanctions on Belarus.
history.why: Urea is made from natural gas, so the European gas crisis shut down fertiliser plants. Then the two largest potash exporters became difficult to buy from.
history.how_long: About eighteen months before prices normalised; the yield effects ran longer.
history.response: India raised subsidies sharply and signed long-term supply agreements with Gulf and Canadian producers. Several countries restricted their own exports, which made the global shortage worse before it got better.
history.lesson: Export restrictions during a shortage are individually rational and collectively disastrous — each country protecting itself shrinks the pool everyone else draws from.

info.name: Fertiliser
info.everyday: Not bought by you — but it decides how much food a farmer can grow, so it sets the price of all of it a season later
info.india: India imports most of its potash and much of its urea. Costly fertiliser becomes either a bigger government subsidy or a smaller harvest, and usually both.

supplies.rank: Largest wheat exporter in the world
supplies.why_now: Wheat keeps flowing, but on terms that can change quickly. Russia has used export duties and informal price floors to steer shipments, and buyers face payment and shipping friction from sanctions even though food itself is exempt. Watch the export duty and any move to restrict volumes.
supplies.what: Russia overtook everyone to become the dominant wheat exporter, and its wheat goes overwhelmingly to countries that cannot easily pay more — Egypt, Turkey, Bangladesh, much of Africa. That makes its harvest a food security variable for a large part of the world.

dependents.detail: The world's largest wheat importer, where bread subsidies are politically foundational
Major buyers with limited alternatives

risks: Frost kill and drought in the main growing regions
Export duties, which Russia uses to keep domestic bread cheap
Payment and shipping friction from sanctions, even though food is exempt
supplies.if_disrupted: World wheat prices rise and the burden lands on low-income importers. Bread price shocks have a long history of producing street protests, and that political effect often matters more than the economic one.
supplies.india: India grows most of its own wheat, so the direct exposure is modest. The indirect effect is that a tight world market pressures India to export — which India resists, having restricted wheat exports since 2022.

history.what: A severe heatwave and wildfires destroyed much of Russia's wheat crop and Russia banned exports. World wheat prices roughly doubled.
history.why: The hottest summer in Russian recorded history. The export ban was imposed to keep domestic bread affordable.
history.how_long: The ban ran about ten months.
history.response: Importers scrambled for US, Australian and Argentine wheat. Egypt and others drew down reserves heavily.
history.lesson: Food price spikes that year contributed to the unrest that became the Arab Spring, which began partly as bread protests. A heatwave in Russia helped topple governments in North Africa — the longest causal chain on this page, and a real one.

info.name: Wheat
info.everyday: Atta, bread, biscuits, noodles, maida
info.india: India mostly grows its own, but world prices still set the floor under domestic wheat and feed into bread and biscuit costs.

supplies.why_now: Supply has continued despite sanctions, but a large share of the world's palladium comes from one sanctioned country and buyers have been designing it out rather than risk it. The amber reflects a dependence being deliberately unwound, not a shortage today.
supplies.what: Palladium is mostly a by-product of Russian nickel mining, which means its supply does not respond to its own price — producers mine it because they are mining something else. That makes shortages unusually hard to fix.

dependents.detail: Every petrol car needs it in the catalytic converter

risks: Sanctions and payment restrictions
Nickel production decisions, which determine palladium output as a side effect
supplies.if_disrupted: Car manufacturing costs rise, and catalytic converter theft becomes more profitable — a surprisingly direct consumer effect seen worldwide during past spikes.
supplies.india: Car manufacturing input costs, and a constraint on meeting tighter emissions norms.

history.what: Palladium spiked to records after the invasion of Ukraine on fears Russian supply would be cut off.
history.why: Roughly 40% of supply came from one sanctioned country, and there is no quick alternative source.
history.how_long: The spike unwound within months as supply kept flowing and carmakers substituted platinum.
history.response: Carmakers accelerated a switch from palladium to platinum, which is cheaper and more available, in catalytic converters.
history.lesson: The threat of losing supply moved the price more than the actual loss did. And substitution, where it is possible at all, is the most durable answer — the palladium price never recovered.

info.name: Palladium & platinum
info.everyday: Catalytic converters that clean car exhaust; platinum also goes into hydrogen equipment
info.india: Car manufacturing input costs, and a genuine constraint on meeting tighter emissions standards.

supplies.why_now: China operates an export licensing regime on rare earths and the magnets made from them. Shipments have largely continued, but each one now needs approval, which means they can be slowed or stopped as leverage without any formal ban being announced — and approvals have been used that way during trade disputes. Buyers outside China are carrying the delay and the uncertainty. This clears only when alternative separation capacity exists at scale, which is a decade-long project.
supplies.what: The misleading thing about rare earths is that they are not rare. They are found in many countries, including India. What is concentrated is the refining — separating them is chemically difficult, dirty and unprofitable at small scale, and China spent thirty years building that capability while everyone else was glad not to.

dependents.detail: Defence, electric vehicles and wind turbines all depend on magnets made from Chinese-refined material
Has diversified since 2010 but remains substantially exposed
Has deposits and almost no separation capacity — it ships ore out and buys magnets back

risks: Export licensing, which China has used repeatedly as leverage
Environmental enforcement closing refining capacity
Retaliation in a broader trade dispute
supplies.if_disrupted: Not an immediate consumer price shock — it is a production stoppage. Electric motor manufacturing, wind turbines, earphones and defence equipment all slow. The damage is measured in delayed factories rather than in a grocery bill, and it takes years rather than months to fix.
supplies.india: Directly relevant to India's electric vehicle and electronics ambitions. India has begun its own rare earth and magnet initiatives for exactly this reason, but building separation capacity is a decade-long project.

history.what: China restricted rare earth exports to Japan during a territorial dispute. Prices of some elements rose more than tenfold.
history.why: A fishing boat collision near disputed islands escalated into an economic measure. It was the first clear demonstration that processing dominance was strategic leverage.
history.how_long: Formal restrictions lasted about two months; the price effects took years to unwind.
history.response: Japan funded recycling, substitution research and alternative supply in Australia — and cut its dependence meaningfully over the following decade. The WTO later ruled against China's export quotas.
history.lesson: This was the moment the world learned that a supply chain can be a weapon. Japan's response is also the template: it took ten years of deliberate investment to reduce the dependence, and it worked — but only because it started immediately.

info.name: Rare earth magnets
info.everyday: Earphones, phone speakers, electric motors, wind turbines, hard drives, defence equipment
info.india: India has deposits but almost no processing. The bottleneck is not the rock — it is who can refine it, and that is overwhelmingly one country.

supplies.share: Dominant in mature-node chips and in assembly
supplies.what: China does not lead at the cutting edge, but it makes an enormous share of the older, simpler chips that go into cars, appliances and industrial equipment — and it assembles most of the world's finished electronics regardless of where the chips were made.

dependents.detail: Assembly capacity at this scale exists nowhere else
Imports a large share of electronic components even for goods assembled in India

risks: Export controls in either direction escalating
Taiwan tensions disrupting the wider regional supply chain
Concentration of assembly in a few industrial clusters
supplies.if_disrupted: Consumer electronics prices rise and launches are delayed. The 2021 shortage showed the car industry is the most fragile link, because a car cannot ship missing one $2 component.
supplies.india: India's electronics assembly growth depends on Chinese components even as it reduces reliance on Chinese finished goods. This is the central tension in the 'make in India' electronics push.

history.what: The global chip shortage halted car assembly lines worldwide and left Indian buyers waiting months for popular models.
history.why: Carmakers cancelled orders expecting a pandemic slump; the capacity was reallocated to consumer electronics, and chip plants take years to build.
history.how_long: About two and a half years.
history.response: Subsidy programmes in the US, EU, Japan and India to build domestic capacity; carmakers moved from just-in-time to holding buffer stocks.
history.lesson: Just-in-time manufacturing is brilliantly efficient and has no shock absorber. After 2021 the world started quietly paying for inventory again.

info.name: Advanced chips
info.everyday: Phones, cars, appliances, ATMs, UPI itself — a modern car has over a thousand
info.india: India designs a lot of chips and manufactures almost none of the advanced ones yet. The 2021 chip shortage left Indian car buyers waiting months.

supplies.what: Aluminium is often called solid electricity: smelting it is so power-hungry that the metal's cost is mostly the cost of the power used to make it. China's dominance is really a dominance of cheap coal power, which is also why its output is vulnerable to power rationing.

dependents.detail: Cans, cars, construction, electricity cables, aircraft
Has its own smelting but competes against Chinese supply on price

risks: Power rationing during droughts in hydro-dependent provinces like Yunnan
Emissions policy capping smelting capacity
Export tax changes
supplies.if_disrupted: Aluminium prices rise worldwide, raising packaging, construction and car costs. Because the constraint is electricity rather than ore, the disruption can arrive with no mining problem at all.
supplies.india: Indian smelters benefit from higher world prices, while Indian manufacturers pay more. India's own smelting is coal-powered, so the same energy-cost logic applies here.

history.what: Chinese power rationing forced aluminium smelters to cut output and world prices hit 13-year highs.
history.why: A coal shortage and emissions targets collided. Smelters in Yunnan, which run on hydropower, were also hit by drought.
history.how_long: About six months.
history.response: China released coal reserves and relaxed production limits. Buyers drew down inventories, which fell to unusually low levels.
history.lesson: Energy policy is metals policy. When a country decides to use less coal, the world pays more for aluminium — the link is not obvious and it is direct.

info.name: Aluminium & bauxite
info.everyday: Cans, foil, window frames, aircraft, electricity cables, and increasingly car bodies
info.india: India has bauxite and significant smelting capacity, so it is a competitor here — but smelting is enormously power-hungry, which ties it to coal prices.

supplies.share: ~65-80% of world output and nearly all battery-grade refining
supplies.why_now: Graphite exports have required permits since 2023, introduced days after new Western restrictions on chip equipment. Material still moves, with added friction and delay. Because nearly all battery-grade processing is Chinese, there is no quick alternative to qualify.
supplies.what: Every lithium-ion battery has more graphite in it than lithium by weight, and almost nobody discusses it. China controls not just mining but the purification and shaping into anode material, which is the hard part.

dependents.who: Every battery and electric vehicle maker in the world
dependents.detail: There is no alternative anode material at scale
Entirely dependent for its battery manufacturing ambitions

risks: Export licensing, which China introduced for graphite in 2023
Environmental enforcement closing processing capacity
supplies.if_disrupted: Battery production slows worldwide. Alternative supply exists in Mozambique, Madagascar and Tanzania, but the refining capacity to turn it into anode material does not — the same pattern as rare earths.
supplies.india: A direct constraint on India's battery manufacturing plans, and a less visible one than lithium because fewer people know to look for it.

history.what: China introduced export permit requirements for graphite products, days after new Western restrictions on chip equipment.
history.why: Widely read as a response in an escalating technology dispute. Graphite was chosen precisely because the dependence is near-total and poorly understood.
history.how_long: Licensing continues; flows have largely continued with added friction and delay.
history.response: Battery makers accelerated qualification of non-Chinese suppliers, a process that takes years because anode material must be tested extensively.
history.lesson: The leverage in a supply chain sits where the processing is, not where the rock is. And the most effective pressure point is the one nobody has been monitoring.

info.name: Graphite
info.everyday: The anode in every lithium-ion battery — the half of the battery nobody talks about
info.india: Imported. There is more graphite than lithium in a battery by weight, and the supply is more concentrated.

supplies.rank: Dominant supplier of the chemicals inside medicines
supplies.why_now: No single incident. Environmental enforcement periodically closes Chinese chemical plants with little notice, and medicine ingredients have been caught in that before. The amber marks how thin the buffer is: the world holds very little inventory of these chemicals.
supplies.what: China makes the active ingredients; India turns many of them into tablets; the world takes the tablets. Two layers of concentration stacked on top of each other, and the lower one is nearly invisible to the patient.

dependents.detail: Imports a large share of the ingredients for the generics it exports to the world
Depend on both layers — Chinese ingredients and Indian formulation

risks: Environmental shutdowns of chemical plants, which China has imposed repeatedly
Export restrictions during a health emergency
Trade disputes reaching into medicine supply
supplies.if_disrupted: Shortages of ordinary medicines — antibiotics, painkillers, blood pressure drugs — across much of the world within months, because the inventory held in the system is thin.
supplies.india: The single biggest vulnerability in India's pharmaceutical industry, and the explicit reason for India's production-linked incentive scheme for key starting materials.

history.what: Chinese environmental enforcement shut large numbers of chemical plants, and prices of some medicine ingredients rose several-fold.
history.why: A sustained campaign against industrial pollution closed plants with inadequate effluent treatment, many of which made pharmaceutical intermediates.
history.how_long: Disruption ran for over a year.
history.response: Indian manufacturers paid far more or reformulated. India later launched incentives to produce key ingredients domestically, with mixed results so far.
history.lesson: A domestic environmental policy in one country became a medicine cost problem everywhere. The world had outsourced the dirty chemistry and forgotten it had done so.

info.name: Medicine ingredients
info.everyday: The active ingredient inside every tablet you take — paracetamol, antibiotics, blood pressure pills
info.india: India makes a fifth of the world's generic medicines by volume but imports a large share of the raw ingredients, mostly from China. The pharmacy of the world buys its chemicals from one supplier.

supplies.what: China grows the most tea but exports a smaller share than India relative to output, because its own consumption absorbs most of it. It dominates green tea in particular.

dependents.detail: Major buyers of Chinese green tea

risks: Spring frost during the first picking, which produces the highest-value leaf
Drought and heatwaves in the southern growing provinces
supplies.if_disrupted: Mostly affects green tea prices and the specific markets that drink it. Less globally systemic than most things on this page.
supplies.india: A competitive matter — Chinese shortfalls lift Indian tea export prices.

history.what: A record heatwave and drought in the Yangtze basin damaged tea and other crops.
history.why: The most severe heatwave in Chinese recorded history dried rivers and reservoirs across the main growing belt.
history.how_long: One season.
history.response: Emergency irrigation and cloud seeding; replanting the following year.
history.lesson: Perennial crops suffer longer than annual ones from a single bad year, because the bush itself is damaged rather than just that year's leaves.

info.name: Tea
info.everyday: The most-drunk prepared beverage on earth after water
info.india: India is both a top-two producer and a huge consumer. Domestic prices are set mostly at home, so this is an export-earnings story rather than an inflation one.

supplies.what: Nothing else on this page is this concentrated. Roughly three-quarters of the world's cobalt comes from one country, much of it from mines with Chinese ownership, and a meaningful share from artisanal workings with serious human rights concerns attached.

dependents.detail: Cobalt stabilises the cathode and extends battery life
Refines the large majority of it, so the dependence is doubled — mined in one country, processed in another
Entirely dependent for electric vehicle and electronics batteries

risks: Political instability and conflict in the mining regions
Export bans — DR Congo has imposed them to force more local processing
Scrutiny of artisanal mining conditions restricting which supply buyers will accept
supplies.if_disrupted: Battery costs rise, which slows the electric vehicle transition everywhere. The industry's defence has been to design cobalt out — lithium iron phosphate batteries use none at all — which is working, and is the clearest example on this page of a dependence being engineered away rather than diversified away.
supplies.india: Electric two-wheeler and car costs. India's battery manufacturing ambitions run straight into this, which is why Indian makers have leaned toward cobalt-free chemistries.

history.what: Cobalt prices spiked sharply in 2018 on electric vehicle demand, then collapsed on oversupply. In 2025 DR Congo imposed export restrictions to support prices and force local refining.
history.why: A small market with concentrated supply and rapidly growing, hard-to-forecast demand. Small changes in either produce violent price swings.
history.how_long: The 2018 spike unwound over about two years.
history.response: Battery chemistry shifted toward lithium iron phosphate, which needs no cobalt at all. Manufacturers also signed direct long-term contracts with miners rather than buying on the market.
history.lesson: The most effective answer to a concentrated supply is often not finding another source — it is redesigning the product so you need less of it. Engineering beat geopolitics here.

info.name: Cobalt
info.everyday: Battery cathodes — the part that decides how long a charge lasts
info.india: Entirely imported, and the supply is more concentrated in one country than almost anything else on this page.

supplies.what: Chile has mined copper for a century and its deposits are ageing — ore grades are falling, which means more rock must be moved for the same metal, using more water in one of the driest places on earth. Its output has been broadly flat for a decade while demand has not been.

dependents.detail: Buys roughly half of all the copper traded in the world
Grids, motors, electric vehicles and data centres all need far more copper per unit than what they replace
Imports copper concentrate; domestic smelting capacity has been constrained since the Sterlite plant closure

risks: Water scarcity and drought in the Atacama, which limits processing
Falling ore grades requiring ever more investment for flat output
Mining royalty and tax changes, and labour disputes at the large mines
supplies.if_disrupted: Copper is the metal the energy transition is built on, and new mines take 10-15 years from discovery to production. A supply problem cannot be answered quickly at any price, which is why many analysts expect structural tightness regardless of any single event.
supplies.india: Construction costs, electrical goods, and the cost of building out the power grid. A sustained copper squeeze makes India's electrification more expensive in a way that compounds over years.

history.what: Strikes at Escondida — the world's largest copper mine — have repeatedly moved the global price. The 2017 strike lasted 44 days and measurably dented world supply.
history.why: Highly concentrated production: a single mine accounts for roughly 5% of world output, so one labour dispute is a global event.
history.how_long: Weeks to months, depending on the dispute.
history.response: Settlements usually involved substantial pay rises. Buyers responded by holding more inventory and signing longer contracts.
history.lesson: When one mine is 5% of world supply, labour relations in one valley become a macroeconomic variable. Watch the wage negotiation calendar, not just the geology.

info.name: Copper
info.everyday: Every wire in your home, every motor, every charger, the electricity grid itself
info.india: India imports copper concentrate. It is also the metal the whole electrification push runs on, so this is a long-term structural dependence, not a passing one.

supplies.what: Palm oil is the most efficient oil crop there is — it yields several times more per hectare than soy or sunflower — which is why it ended up in roughly half the packaged products in a supermarket. Indonesia and Malaysia together produce about 85% of it, which is a remarkable concentration for something so widely used.

dependents.detail: The largest importer in the world, and palm is the cheapest cooking oil for Indian households
Major buyers for cooking and food processing
Biscuits, instant noodles, soap, cosmetics, chocolate

risks: Export levies and outright bans to control domestic cooking oil prices
Biodiesel mandates diverting palm oil from food into fuel — Indonesia's B40 programme does exactly this
El Niño reducing yields, with the effect showing up 6-12 months later
EU deforestation rules restricting which plantations can sell into Europe
supplies.if_disrupted: Cooking oil prices rise fastest and most visibly of anything on this page, because the supply is concentrated, the demand is non-negotiable and there is no close substitute at the price. Sunflower and soy oil then rise too, as buyers switch.
supplies.india: This is arguably the most direct line on the whole page between a foreign policy decision and an Indian kitchen. India imports around 60% of its edible oil, mostly palm from Indonesia and Malaysia, so an Indonesian export levy shows up in Indian grocery prices within weeks.

history.what: Indonesia banned palm oil exports outright to bring down its own domestic cooking oil prices. World prices hit record highs.
history.why: Domestic cooking oil had become unaffordable and there had been protests. The government chose its own consumers over its export earnings — an entirely predictable political choice.
history.how_long: The ban lasted about three weeks before being lifted, but export levies and domestic market obligations continued for months.
history.response: India accelerated purchases from Malaysia and cut its own import duties to cushion households. Indonesia replaced the ban with a 'domestic market obligation' requiring exporters to sell a share locally first.
history.lesson: A producing country will always protect its own consumers first. Any import dependence on a single country for a politically sensitive food is a standing risk, and the warning sign is unrest in the producing country, not a crop failure.

info.name: Palm oil
info.everyday: The cheapest cooking oil, plus soap, biscuits, chocolate, instant noodles and cosmetics
info.india: India is the world's biggest buyer of edible oils and imports roughly 60% of what it uses, most of it palm. A palm oil shock reaches an Indian kitchen within weeks.

supplies.why_now: Indonesia keeps adjusting the rules — royalties, permitted output and processing requirements have all changed recently — and because it now supplies over half the world's nickel, each change moves the global price. The risk here is policy, not geology.
supplies.what: Indonesia went from a modest producer to over half the world's supply in under a decade by banning raw ore exports and forcing smelters to be built on its own soil. It is the most successful resource-nationalism policy of recent times, and it worked exactly as intended.

dependents.detail: Owns or finances most of the Indonesian smelting capacity
Two-thirds of nickel goes into stainless steel, not batteries
Higher-nickel cathodes give electric vehicles longer range

risks: Export policy changes, which Indonesia has shown it will use
Environmental objections to nickel processing, which is energy-intensive and polluting
Oversupply crushing prices and forcing mine closures elsewhere, which concentrates supply further
supplies.if_disrupted: Stainless steel and battery costs rise. The subtler risk is the opposite: Indonesian oversupply has driven prices so low that producers in other countries have shut, which makes the world more dependent on Indonesia with every passing year.
supplies.india: Stainless steel manufacturing and the battery supply chain India is trying to build. India imports essentially all of its nickel.

history.what: Indonesia banned raw nickel ore exports outright in 2020 to force domestic processing. In March 2022 the nickel price doubled in a day on the London Metal Exchange and trading was suspended.
history.why: The 2020 ban was industrial policy. The 2022 spike was a short squeeze — a large producer had bet against the price and could not meet margin calls, and the exchange cancelled trades, which badly damaged its credibility.
history.how_long: The ore ban is permanent; the 2022 squeeze lasted days but the reputational damage persists.
history.response: Indonesia's policy attracted enormous Chinese investment in local smelting. The LME faced lawsuits and reformed its position-limit rules.
history.lesson: Two lessons in one commodity. A resource-rich country can successfully force processing onshore — and a commodity market can break for reasons that have nothing to do with supply at all.

info.name: Nickel
info.everyday: Stainless steel — sinks, cutlery, utensils — and the cathode in longer-range electric vehicle batteries
info.india: Almost entirely imported, for both stainless steel manufacturing and the battery supply chain India is trying to build.

supplies.share: Largest thermal coal exporter in the world
supplies.rank: Dominant in the seaborne thermal market
supplies.what: Indonesian coal is lower in energy content but cheap and close to Asia's power stations, which makes it the default fuel for much of the region's electricity.

dependents.detail: A major buyer; Indian power plants are configured to blend imported Indonesian coal with domestic supply
Large importers for power generation

risks: Domestic market obligations — Indonesia has banned exports outright to keep its own power stations running
Heavy rain disrupting open-cast mining and barge transport
Energy transition policy reducing long-term demand
supplies.if_disrupted: Electricity costs rise across Asia and power cuts become likely in countries running thin coal stocks. This is one of the fastest-acting items on the page, because coal stockpiles at power stations are typically measured in days.
supplies.india: Direct and serious. India has had power crises caused by coal shortages, and imported Indonesian coal is part of how they are resolved.

history.what: Indonesia banned all coal exports for a month, at a few days' notice, to refill its own power stations.
history.why: Domestic power producers had not met their stockpile obligations and Indonesia faced the risk of widespread blackouts.
history.how_long: About a month, eased in stages.
history.response: Importing countries including India scrambled for Australian and South African coal at much higher prices. Indonesia tightened enforcement of its domestic market obligation.
history.lesson: A country facing its own blackouts will cut exports with almost no notice. Energy security beats trade commitments every time, and a few days' warning is all you get.

info.name: Coal
info.everyday: Electricity, and the heat that makes steel and cement
info.india: India mines a great deal and still imports more, because domestic coal is lower quality. Coal shortages have caused Indian power cuts repeatedly.

supplies.what: Natural rubber cannot be fully replaced by synthetic in heavy-duty tyres — truck and aircraft tyres need the real thing for heat resistance. Most of it is grown by smallholders on trees that take seven years to mature.

dependents.detail: The dominant use by far
A major tyre producer and a net importer of rubber

risks: Leaf disease outbreaks, which have hit Indonesian plantations
Low prices discouraging tapping — smallholders simply stop when it is not worth the labour
Ageing trees and slow replanting
supplies.if_disrupted: Tyre costs rise, which feeds into vehicle prices and freight costs. The seven-year maturity means supply cannot respond quickly to any price.
supplies.india: Indian tyre makers' input costs, and therefore the cost of running every truck on Indian roads — which is an input to the price of everything that moves.

history.what: Rubber prices hit multi-year highs as disease, floods and years of under-tapping cut supply from Thailand and Indonesia.
history.why: Prices had been low for a decade, so smallholders had stopped tapping and had not replanted. When demand recovered, the trees were not there.
history.how_long: Ongoing tightness; replanting takes seven years to show up.
history.response: Tyre makers raised prices and sought synthetic substitution where technically possible.
history.lesson: A decade of low prices creates a shortage a decade later. With tree crops the damage is done quietly, during the years when everything looks abundant.

info.name: Natural rubber
info.everyday: Tyres above all — a truck tyre needs natural rubber that synthetic cannot replace — plus gloves, footwear and seals
info.india: India is a major tyre manufacturer and a net importer of rubber. Kerala grows some, nowhere near enough.

supplies.rank: Largest producer by a wide margin
supplies.what: Brazil grows most of the world's arabica, the bean in better-quality coffee. Coffee trees are unusually vulnerable: a single frost can damage a tree for several years, not just one harvest, so one bad night affects supply for a long time afterwards.

dependents.detail: The largest consuming markets
Menu prices follow the bean with a lag of months
Grows and exports its own coffee, so an Indian grower gains when Brazil suffers

risks: Frost in the growing regions, historically the single biggest factor
Drought during flowering, which sets the following year's crop
The natural two-year on-off cycle of arabica yields
supplies.if_disrupted: Coffee is a textbook case of a slow shock. The price moves immediately, but your café does not change its menu for six to twelve months, so the consumer feels it long after the news.
supplies.india: A rare case where a foreign crop failure helps India — Indian coffee exporters earn more. Indian consumers of imported coffee pay more.

history.what: The 1975 'Black Frost' destroyed a large share of Brazil's coffee trees and prices roughly quadrupled. In 2021, frost and drought together pushed arabica to multi-year highs.
history.why: Coffee grows in a narrow climate band. Trees take three to four years to bear fruit, so lost trees cannot be replaced within a season at any price.
history.how_long: The 1975 effects ran for several years; the 2021 episode took about two years to normalise.
history.response: Growers replanted in less frost-prone areas and at different altitudes; roasters blended more robusta — the hardier, cheaper bean — into their products.
history.lesson: With tree crops, the recovery time is set by biology, not by markets. Watch how long the plant takes to mature: that is the real duration of the shock.

info.name: Coffee
info.everyday: Your cup, and the price on every café menu
info.india: India grows and exports coffee, so a Brazilian frost is good news for Indian growers and bad news for Indian drinkers.

supplies.what: Brazilian ore is unusually high grade, which matters because higher grade means less energy to smelt — increasingly valuable as steelmakers try to cut emissions. Most of it travels a very long way to China.

dependents.detail: Buys the majority of seaborne iron ore to feed more than half the world's steel production

risks: Tailings dam failures, which have twice caused disasters and suspended large operations
Heavy rain in the mining regions disrupting rail and ports
Chinese construction demand, which is the whole demand side of this market
supplies.if_disrupted: Steel prices rise globally, raising construction and manufacturing costs. Unusually for this page, Indian steel producers benefit.
supplies.india: India has its own ore and is a large steel producer, so a Brazilian disruption lifts Indian steel company profits while raising the cost of Indian construction. The two effects land on different people.

history.what: The Brumadinho tailings dam collapsed, killing 270 people. Vale suspended operations across several sites and iron ore prices rose roughly 30%.
history.why: A dam built by the cheaper 'upstream' method failed. The same company had suffered a similar disaster at Mariana in 2015 — the warning had already been delivered.
history.how_long: Prices stayed elevated for most of 2019; some capacity never returned.
history.response: Brazil banned upstream tailings dams and ordered existing ones decommissioned. Mining regulation was tightened substantially across the industry.
history.lesson: Safety failures are supply events. A disaster that kills people also removes production for years, and the regulation that follows removes more.

info.name: Iron ore & steel
info.everyday: Buildings, cars, bridges, railways, the cost of construction
info.india: India has its own iron ore and is a major steel producer, so here India is a competitor rather than a dependent — world steel prices set Indian steel company profits.

supplies.share: ~22% of world production, ~45-50% of world exports
supplies.rank: Largest producer and by far the largest exporter
supplies.what: Brazil is unusual: its mills can switch between making sugar and making ethanol for cars depending on which pays better that week. That means the world sugar price is partly set by the Brazilian petrol price, which is a genuinely strange causal chain and a real one.

dependents.detail: Large importers in deficit years
Heavy structural importers with little domestic cane
Sugar is an input to most packaged food

risks: Drought or frost in the centre-south cane belt
The sugar-versus-ethanol switch, driven by oil prices and fuel taxes
A weak real, which encourages exports and caps world prices
supplies.if_disrupted: World sugar prices rise quickly because the exportable surplus is so concentrated here. Sweets, soft drinks and biscuits follow with a lag of a few months as manufacturers work through contracted stock.
supplies.india: India is the second producer and a swing exporter, so Brazilian problems lift Indian sugar mill profits and Indian export earnings — while raising what Indian consumers pay if domestic supply is also tight. The two effects land on different people, which is why sugar policy is contested.

history.what: World sugar hit a 12-year high after poor monsoon rains cut Indian output and India restricted exports, leaving the market dependent on Brazil.
history.why: An El Niño year reduced Indian cane yields. India restricted exports to protect domestic prices, removing the second largest exporter from the market at the same time.
history.how_long: About a year, easing as a strong Brazilian crop arrived in 2024.
history.response: India diverted cane to ethanol to support farmer incomes, then eased that too when sugar ran short. Brazil expanded crushing capacity to capture the high prices.
history.lesson: Two producers dominate exports, and when one steps back the other has to carry the world. Watch whether India is exporting — that single fact moves the global sugar price more than anything happening in Brazil.

info.name: Sugar
info.everyday: Sweets, soft drinks, biscuits, and — through ethanol — a slice of your petrol
info.india: India is both a huge producer and a swing exporter. Policy here moves the world price, and the world price moves Indian sugar company profits.

supplies.rank: Overtook the United States to become the dominant supplier
supplies.what: Soy is mostly not eaten by people. It is crushed into meal that feeds chickens and pigs, and oil that goes into cooking. So the soy price is really the price of chicken and eggs a few months later, which is how a Brazilian drought becomes a protein cost in Asia.

dependents.detail: Buys roughly 60% of all soybeans traded in the world, almost entirely to feed pigs
Imports soy oil as part of the edible oil basket; soymeal prices set Indian poultry feed costs

risks: Drought in the Mato Grosso and southern growing regions
Chinese demand, which is one buyer deciding most of the market
Road and port bottlenecks — much of the crop travels enormous distances on poor roads
supplies.if_disrupted: Edible oil and animal feed prices rise together, which is unusually broad: it pushes up cooking oil, chicken, eggs and milk at the same time.
supplies.india: A direct line to two Indian grocery items at once — the cooking oil bottle and the chicken. Indian poultry margins are set substantially by a crop grown in South America.

history.what: A severe drought in southern Brazil and Argentina cut the harvest sharply and soy oil prices hit records, compounding the Ukraine sunflower oil shortage.
history.why: A La Niña year brought drought to exactly the region that supplies most of the world's soy, at the same time as Black Sea sunflower oil stopped moving.
history.how_long: About 18 months.
history.response: India cut edible oil import duties to cushion households and leaned harder on palm oil. Brazil expanded planted area the following season.
history.lesson: Edible oils are substitutes, which sounds reassuring and is not: when one fails, buyers crowd into the others and they all rise together. There is no diversification within a category that moves as one.

info.name: Soybeans & soy oil
info.everyday: Cooking oil, and — as animal feed — the real cost behind chicken, eggs and milk
info.india: India imports soy oil as part of its edible oil basket, and soymeal prices feed straight into Indian poultry and dairy costs.

supplies.rank: Second exporter after the United States
supplies.what: Brazil's second corn crop, planted after soybeans are harvested, has turned it into a major exporter in about fifteen years. That double cropping is an impressive agricultural achievement and a fragile one — it depends on the rains arriving on schedule twice.

dependents.detail: Large feed importers
Corn is the main feed grain

risks: Late rains delaying soybean harvest, which compresses the corn planting window
Drought during the second crop's growing season
supplies.if_disrupted: Feed prices rise, and chicken, eggs and pork follow within a few months. Corn shortages are felt as meat inflation rather than as corn inflation, which is why they are often misattributed.
supplies.india: India mostly grows its own, but world corn prices set the floor under Indian poultry feed, and India has begun importing corn for ethanol — a new and growing exposure.

history.what: Drought and frost cut Brazil's second corn crop by roughly a quarter and world corn prices rose sharply.
history.why: A dry La Niña season followed by an unusually late frost hit the crop at its most vulnerable stage.
history.how_long: About a year.
history.response: Importers switched to US and Argentine supply; Brazilian farmers expanded area the following year.
history.lesson: Double cropping raises output and removes the margin for error. Squeezing two harvests into one year means a two-week delay can cost an entire crop.

info.name: Corn (maize)
info.everyday: Animal feed first, then starch, sweeteners and ethanol — most of it is eaten by livestock, not people
info.india: India grows most of what it uses, but world corn prices set the cost of poultry feed, which is why chicken prices track a crop grown in Iowa.

supplies.what: Almost all of it comes from one region — the Pilbara in Western Australia — and travels to China. This is one of the largest and most concentrated single trade flows on earth, and it is the reason Australia's economy tracks Chinese construction.

dependents.detail: Buys the large majority of Australian ore; it is the backbone of Chinese steelmaking
Significant buyers for their own steel industries

risks: Cyclones in the Pilbara, which shut ports for days at a time
Chinese property construction, which drives the entire demand side
Diplomatic friction between Australia and China
supplies.if_disrupted: Global steel prices rise. Because the flow is so large and so concentrated, even a week of closed ports is visible in the world price.
supplies.india: Indian steelmakers gain from higher global prices; Indian construction pays more. India is largely self-sufficient in ore, so this is a profit story rather than a supply story.

history.what: Iron ore reached record highs above $230 a tonne, then halved within months.
history.why: Chinese stimulus after the pandemic drove enormous steel demand, then Beijing ordered steel output cuts for emissions reasons and the property sector began its long decline.
history.how_long: The round trip took about six months.
history.response: Miners used the windfall to pay down debt and return cash rather than expand, having been burned by the previous cycle.
history.lesson: For a commodity with one dominant buyer, the demand side is the risk, not the supply side. Watch Chinese construction starts, not Australian weather.

info.name: Iron ore & steel
info.everyday: Buildings, cars, bridges, railways, the cost of construction
info.india: India has its own iron ore and is a major steel producer, so here India is a competitor rather than a dependent — world steel prices set Indian steel company profits.

supplies.rank: Largest miner; most of it is refined in China
supplies.what: Australia mines the rock, China converts it into battery-grade chemicals. That split is the whole story: mining is diversified and refining is not, so controlling the mine does not control the supply chain.

dependents.detail: Refines the overwhelming majority of the world's lithium regardless of where it was mined

dependents.who: Every battery and electric vehicle maker
dependents.detail: There is no substitute for lithium in current battery chemistry

risks: Violent price cycles — lithium rose roughly tenfold in 2021-22 then fell about 80%
Refining concentration meaning mine diversification does not help much
Mine closures when prices collapse, which sets up the next shortage
supplies.if_disrupted: Battery and electric vehicle costs rise. The deeper problem is the cycle: low prices shut mines, which guarantees the next shortage, which causes the next spike.
supplies.india: Every electric scooter and car sold in India contains imported lithium. India has signed exploration agreements abroad and found domestic deposits, but refining capacity is the real gap and it does not exist yet.

history.what: Lithium prices rose roughly tenfold, then fell about 80% as new supply arrived and electric vehicle demand growth slowed.
history.why: A small market meeting enormous, rapidly growing demand. Mines take years to open, so the response always overshoots in both directions.
history.how_long: Up over 18 months, down over about 24.
history.response: Carmakers signed direct offtake agreements with miners and some bought stakes in mines outright, abandoning the idea that they could simply buy materials on the market.
history.lesson: In small markets with long lead times, the cure for high prices is high prices — and the cure for low prices is low prices. The cycle is the system working, not failing.

info.name: Lithium
info.everyday: Phone batteries, laptop batteries, electric scooters and cars, grid storage
info.india: India imports essentially all of it. Every electric vehicle sold in India contains someone else's lithium.

supplies.share: Largest metallurgical coal exporter in the world
supplies.what: Australia dominates the coking coal used to make steel, which is a different market from thermal coal for power and has no ready substitute — you cannot currently make steel at scale in a blast furnace without it.

dependents.detail: Indian steelmakers are among the largest buyers; India has little coking coal of its own
Major steel producers

risks: Cyclones and flooding in Queensland, which have repeatedly shut mines and rail lines
Diplomatic disputes — China informally banned Australian coal for about two years
Investment decline as banks withdraw from coal financing, which constrains future supply
supplies.if_disrupted: Steelmaking costs rise worldwide, which raises construction and manufacturing costs. Indian steel producers are unusually exposed because they import most of their coking coal.
supplies.india: One of India's most direct and least-discussed import dependencies. India's steel ambitions run on Australian coal, and there is no domestic substitute of the required quality.

history.what: China informally banned Australian coal imports amid a diplomatic dispute. Trade flows reorganised entirely, with Australian coal going to India and Japan, and China buying from Russia and Indonesia.
history.why: A political dispute following Australia's call for an inquiry into the origins of Covid-19.
history.how_long: About three years before trade resumed.
history.response: Both sides found alternatives, at a cost. Chinese power plants faced shortages; Australian exporters found new buyers, with India a major beneficiary.
history.lesson: Trade bans hurt both sides and rarely achieve their aim, but they do permanently rewire who buys from whom. India got cheaper coking coal out of a dispute it had nothing to do with.

info.name: Coal
info.everyday: Electricity, and the heat that makes steel and cement
info.india: India mines a great deal and still imports more, because domestic coal is lower quality. Coal shortages have caused Indian power cuts repeatedly.

supplies.what: This is the one place on this page where India is the chokepoint rather than the dependent. India exports more rice than the next four exporters combined, much of it to countries in Africa and Asia with few alternatives and little ability to pay more.

dependents.detail: Benin, Senegal and others rely heavily on Indian parboiled rice
Immediate neighbours who buy when their own crops fall short
The main market for Indian basmati

risks: A weak monsoon reducing the crop
Domestic food inflation prompting export restrictions — the usual trigger
Elections, which make food price control politically urgent
supplies.if_disrupted: World rice prices rise sharply and the effect concentrates on countries that can least absorb it. Unlike wheat, the rice market is thin — only a small share of world production is traded — so a modest change in India's exports moves the price a great deal.
supplies.india: Domestically the opposite: export restrictions are imposed precisely to keep Indian rice cheap, so Indian consumers benefit while Indian farmers and exporters lose. The policy is a transfer between Indians as much as a measure against the world.

history.what: India banned exports of non-basmati white rice. World rice prices rose to their highest in about 15 years and buyers across Africa and Asia scrambled.
history.why: An uneven monsoon and rising domestic food inflation before a general election. The government chose domestic prices over export earnings.
history.how_long: Restrictions ran for roughly 14 months before being substantially eased in late 2024.
history.response: India made government-to-government exceptions for countries in genuine need. Importers turned to Thailand and Vietnam, whose prices rose accordingly.
history.lesson: The same pattern as Indonesian palm oil, with the roles reversed — and worth remembering when reading about other countries' export bans. Every government does this. It is not a betrayal of trade, it is what trade policy is for.

info.name: Rice
info.everyday: The staple on half the world's plates
info.india: India is the largest exporter, so here the risk runs the other way: when India restricts exports to protect its own prices, the shortage lands on buyers in Africa and Asia.

supplies.share: Not a producer — the second largest consumer
supplies.rank: Roughly a quarter of world jewellery demand
supplies.what: India is included here as the demand-side chokepoint. Indian wedding and festival buying is large enough to move the world gold price, and Indian import duty decisions change world flows.

dependents.detail: Swiss refineries reshape bars specifically for Indian and Chinese demand

risks: Import duty changes, which shift demand between official and unofficial channels
A weak monsoon reducing rural incomes, which is a large share of gold demand
supplies.if_disrupted: Indian demand falling is one of the few things that reliably softens the world gold price.
supplies.india: Gold is the second largest item on India's import bill after crude. High gold prices widen the trade deficit and weaken the rupee — a rare case where a household saving habit becomes a macroeconomic problem.

history.what: India raised gold import duty to 10% and imposed the '80:20' rule requiring a fifth of imports to be re-exported.
history.why: The current account deficit had reached a crisis level during the taper tantrum, and gold imports were the second largest cause.
history.how_long: Restrictions eased from 2014; the duty took far longer to normalise.
history.response: Duty increases, import quotas, plus the later launch of Sovereign Gold Bonds to offer a paper alternative to physical buying.
history.lesson: It worked on the trade deficit and created a large smuggling industry at the same time. Restricting something people genuinely want moves it out of sight rather than removing it.

info.name: Gold
info.everyday: Jewellery, weddings, and the thing Indian households save in when they trust nothing else
info.india: India is the second largest consumer in the world and produces almost none of it. Gold imports are the second biggest item on the import bill after oil.

supplies.rank: Second largest producer; a swing exporter
supplies.what: India's sugar is as much a political programme as an industry. The government sets a minimum price mills must pay farmers, which protects growers and regularly leaves mills unable to pay. Cane is also extremely thirsty, grown heavily in states where water is scarce.

dependents.who: Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Indonesia, East Africa
dependents.detail: Regular buyers of Indian sugar when exports are allowed
Whether India exports is one of the two biggest variables in global sugar

risks: A weak monsoon reducing cane yields in Maharashtra and Karnataka
Export restrictions when domestic prices rise
The ethanol diversion programme, which takes cane away from sugar
supplies.if_disrupted: Because India and Brazil dominate exports, India stepping back leaves the world dependent on one supplier and prices rise sharply — exactly what happened in 2023.
supplies.india: Domestically this is a three-way tug of war between farmers who want a high cane price, mills caught in the middle, and consumers and the government who want cheap sugar. Policy swings between them, and sugar company profits swing with it.

history.what: India restricted sugar exports after a poor monsoon. World prices reached a 12-year high.
history.why: El Niño cut cane yields in the main growing states while the ethanol programme was also absorbing cane. Domestic food inflation was already a political problem.
history.how_long: Restrictions ran for about 18 months before being eased in 2025.
history.response: Exports capped, ethanol diversion limits adjusted mid-season, and mills directed to prioritise sugar over ethanol when stocks looked thin.
history.lesson: A government with a food inflation problem will always choose domestic prices over export earnings. This is the same decision Indonesia made with palm oil — the roles simply reverse depending on what is scarce.

info.name: Sugar
info.everyday: Sweets, soft drinks, biscuits, and — through ethanol — a slice of your petrol
info.india: India is both a huge producer and a swing exporter. Policy here moves the world price, and the world price moves Indian sugar company profits.

supplies.what: Nothing else on this page is as concentrated in India as this. Chilli, turmeric, cumin, coriander, pepper and cardamom all come overwhelmingly from Indian farms, grown mostly on small holdings with little mechanisation and heavy weather exposure.

dependents.detail: Seasonings, sauces, instant foods and ready meals
The main importing markets

risks: Unseasonal rain at harvest, which ruins drying and quality
Pesticide residue rejections by EU and US regulators, which can shut a market overnight
Heatwaves during flowering
supplies.if_disrupted: Spice prices are volatile and rise fast, because production is concentrated and demand is inelastic — nobody stops buying turmeric because it got dearer.
supplies.india: Spices are a visible part of Indian food inflation and a meaningful export earner. Cumin prices more than doubled in 2023 after a poor harvest, which showed up directly in household budgets.

history.what: Cumin prices roughly tripled to record highs after a poor Indian harvest, and India briefly became an importer of a spice it normally dominates.
history.why: Unseasonal rain and a smaller planted area in Gujarat and Rajasthan, combined with low carryover stocks from the previous year.
history.how_long: About a year, until a larger 2024 crop arrived.
history.response: Farmers expanded planting sharply in response to the price — which then caused a glut and a price collapse the following season.
history.lesson: In crops with a short planting cycle, a price spike contains its own cure and its own next crisis. The farmer planting in response to high prices is why the price will be low next year.

info.name: Spices
info.everyday: Chilli, turmeric, cumin, pepper, cardamom — the base of most of the world's cooking
info.india: India dominates this more completely than it dominates anything else. Here India IS the supply risk for everyone else.

supplies.rank: Second largest producer and a major exporter
supplies.what: Assam and Darjeeling in the north and the Nilgiris in the south. Tea is a plantation crop with a long replanting cycle and an ageing bush profile in many Indian estates, which quietly caps yields.

dependents.detail: The main buyers of Indian tea

risks: Erratic monsoon and rising temperatures in Assam, which is already near the crop's heat limit
Labour costs and estate economics, which have squeezed replanting investment
Pesticide residue standards in importing markets
supplies.if_disrupted: Tea prices rise, mostly in the producing and immediately neighbouring regions. The world market is less concentrated than coffee, so the effect is more regional.
supplies.india: Mostly a domestic and export-earnings story: India drinks most of what it grows. Tea prices feed into household budgets quietly but persistently.

history.what: Pandemic lockdowns stopped plucking during the critical first flush, and tea prices rose sharply.
history.why: Tea must be plucked on a short cycle; leaves left on the bush are lost. A few weeks of closure removed an entire grade of the crop.
history.how_long: About a year.
history.response: Estates were classified as essential activity and allowed to operate with reduced workforces.
history.lesson: For crops with a narrow harvest window, labour availability is the supply chain. The plants were fine; nobody could pick them.

info.name: Tea
info.everyday: The most-drunk prepared beverage on earth after water
info.india: India is both a top-two producer and a huge consumer. Domestic prices are set mostly at home, so this is an export-earnings story rather than an inflation one.

supplies.share: ~20% of world generic medicines by volume
supplies.rank: The largest supplier of generic drugs in the world
supplies.why_now: India's generic industry is running normally, but it buys a large share of its raw chemicals from China, so it inherits that exposure. The amber is for the dependency inside the strength, not for a current shortage.
supplies.what: India is called the pharmacy of the world and the description is accurate — but it buys a large share of the chemical ingredients it formulates from China. India makes the tablet; China often makes what is in it. That is the dependency inside the strength.

dependents.detail: A very large share of HIV, tuberculosis and malaria medicines come from India
A large share of generic prescriptions filled are Indian-made
India produces a very large share of the world's vaccine doses

risks: Chinese ingredient supply, which is the upstream bottleneck
US FDA inspection findings, which can shut a plant's export market overnight
Export restrictions during a health emergency
supplies.if_disrupted: Medicine shortages and price rises in dozens of countries that have no alternative supplier at this price. Of everything on this page, this is the one where disruption costs lives rather than money.
supplies.india: A major export industry and a strategic vulnerability at once. India has launched production-linked incentives specifically to make key ingredients domestically, for exactly this reason.

history.what: India restricted exports of 26 drug ingredients and formulations, including paracetamol, early in the pandemic.
history.why: Chinese ingredient plants had shut during its own outbreak, and India feared it would run short for its own population.
history.how_long: Most restrictions were lifted within a few months.
history.response: Restrictions eased as Chinese supply resumed. India then launched incentive schemes to manufacture key ingredients domestically.
history.lesson: The world discovered that the pharmacy of the world depends on one chemical supplier. A supply chain is only as diversified as its deepest layer, and almost nobody looks that far down until it fails.

info.name: Medicine ingredients
info.everyday: The active ingredient inside every tablet you take — paracetamol, antibiotics, blood pressure pills
info.india: India makes a fifth of the world's generic medicines by volume but imports a large share of the raw ingredients, mostly from China. The pharmacy of the world buys its chemicals from one supplier.

supplies.what: Cotton underpins India's textile industry, which is among the country's largest employers after agriculture. Most of it is grown rain-fed on smallholdings, which makes the crop unusually monsoon-sensitive.

dependents.detail: Garment manufacturing hubs that import Indian cotton and yarn
A large buyer in deficit years

risks: Pink bollworm infestations, a recurring problem
Monsoon failure in Gujarat and Maharashtra
Import duty changes, which Indian mills lobby against and farmers lobby for
supplies.if_disrupted: Yarn and fabric prices rise, which raises clothing costs — a visible and widely-felt consumer item — and squeezes garment manufacturers in neighbouring countries.
supplies.india: A genuine conflict of interest within India: farmers want high cotton prices, textile mills want low ones. Government policy swings between them and both sides lobby hard.

history.what: Cotton prices hit record highs in India as a poor crop met strong post-pandemic textile demand. Mills cut production because they could not afford raw material.
history.why: Pink bollworm damage and unseasonal rain cut yields just as global clothing demand rebounded sharply.
history.how_long: About a year.
history.response: India scrapped the 11% cotton import duty for several months to help mills — directly against farmer interests, and reversed once prices fell.
history.lesson: When a country both grows and processes a commodity, policy cannot help one side without hurting the other. Watch which lobby is winning; it tells you the direction of the next policy change.

info.name: Cotton
info.everyday: Clothing, bedsheets, towels — roughly a quarter of the world's fibre
info.india: India is a top producer and the backbone of its textile industry, which is one of the country's largest employers after agriculture.

supplies.share: ~20% of world production, a top-two exporter
supplies.what: Included because of what it does politically rather than its size. Onions store badly, the crop arrives in distinct seasons, and the price can triple within weeks when a harvest is damaged. In India that is not a grocery story, it is a political one.

dependents.detail: Heavily dependent on Indian onions; prices there spike within days of an Indian export ban

risks: Unseasonal rain damaging the stored rabi crop or the arriving kharif crop
Export bans, which India imposes almost reflexively when prices rise
supplies.if_disrupted: Neighbouring countries feel it immediately and severely, because they have no alternative supplier at a comparable distance or price.
supplies.india: Onion prices have been a factor in state election results more than once. Governments act on them faster than on almost any other price, which is why export bans arrive so quickly.

history.what: India imposed a 40% export duty, then a minimum export price, then an outright ban on onion exports. Prices in Bangladesh and Nepal rose several-fold.
history.why: Unseasonal rain damaged the stored crop and domestic prices were climbing ahead of elections.
history.how_long: Restrictions in various forms ran for about a year.
