history.response: Buffer stock releases, imports from Egypt and Turkey, and staged easing of the ban after the harvest arrived.
history.lesson: The speed of the policy response is proportional to the political sensitivity of the item, not its economic importance. Onions get acted on in days; fertiliser takes a season.

info.name: Onions
info.everyday: Unremarkable everywhere else; politically explosive in India
info.india: Onion prices have contributed to governments losing elections in India. No other vegetable carries this much political weight.

supplies.rank: Largest producer; with Ghana, about 60% of world supply
supplies.why_now: Prices came down from the 2024 record as the 2025 crop improved, but the underlying problem has not been fixed: the trees are old, swollen shoot disease is still spreading, and farmer payments have only recently risen enough to justify replanting — which takes years to show up as beans. Another poor season would move prices sharply again.
supplies.what: Most of the world's chocolate begins on smallholder farms in two neighbouring West African countries, grown on ageing trees by farmers earning very little. That combination — concentration plus poverty plus old trees — is why this supply is fragile.

dependents.detail: The main processing and consuming region
There is no alternative growing region at this scale
Imports essentially all its cocoa; a small but rapidly growing chocolate market

risks: Harmattan winds and drought during the growing season
Swollen shoot virus and black pod disease, both spreading in ageing plantations
Farmer poverty discouraging replanting, which guarantees falling yields later
Smuggling across borders when one country's fixed farmgate price is higher
supplies.if_disrupted: Chocolate prices rise with a long lag, and manufacturers respond first by shrinking the bar rather than raising the price — which is why the 2024 shock was visible on shelves as smaller products.
supplies.india: Imported chocolate and confectionery costs. Minor in the inflation basket, but one of the clearest examples of a distant farm problem reaching an Indian shop.

history.what: Cocoa prices more than tripled to records above $10,000 a tonne — the largest move in the market's history.
history.why: Three consecutive poor harvests from heavy rain then drought, worsened by swollen shoot disease and by years of under-investment because farmers were paid too little to replant.
history.how_long: Prices stayed extreme through 2024 and eased only gradually as the 2025 crop improved.
history.response: Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire raised farmgate prices substantially to encourage replanting. The EU delayed its deforestation regulation, which would have further restricted supply. Manufacturers reduced pack sizes and substituted other ingredients.
history.lesson: This shortage was decades in the making. Farmers paid too little cannot invest in their trees, and the yield decline that follows is invisible until it is a crisis. Chronic under-investment looks like stability right up until it does not.

info.name: Cocoa
info.everyday: Chocolate, and anything with chocolate in it
info.india: Almost entirely imported. The 2024 cocoa price spike is the reason chocolate bars quietly shrank.

supplies.rank: Among the top two LNG exporters
supplies.what: Qatar's gas comes from the North Field, the largest single gas field in the world, shared with Iran. Its cost of production is among the lowest anywhere, which makes it the supplier of last resort when Europe or Asia is short — and every cargo must leave through Hormuz.

dependents.detail: Became a major buyer after Russian pipeline gas was cut
Long-standing contracted buyers
Petronet's long-term Qatari contract is the backbone of Indian LNG supply

risks: Hormuz, which every single cargo must transit — there is no pipeline alternative
Regional conflict
Competition from US LNG, which is a commercial rather than a supply risk
supplies.if_disrupted: Europe and Asia would bid against each other for a shrunken pool of cargoes, exactly as they did in 2022. Spot LNG prices can rise several hundred percent when that happens, because in the short run there is almost no way to make more.
supplies.india: Cooking gas, piped gas, power generation costs and — importantly — fertiliser, which is made from natural gas. India's long-term Qatari contract is protective precisely because it is not exposed to the spot price.

history.what: European spot gas prices rose more than tenfold after Russian pipeline supply was cut, and LNG cargoes were diverted from Asia to Europe by price.
history.why: Europe had to replace pipeline gas with seaborne LNG almost overnight, and the world LNG fleet and liquefaction capacity simply were not large enough.
history.how_long: About a year of extreme prices; structurally changed by 2024 as new supply arrived.
history.response: Europe built floating import terminals in months rather than years, cut demand sharply, and signed long-term contracts with Qatar and the US. Asian buyers with long-term contracts were largely protected; those buying spot were not.
history.lesson: Long-term contracts look expensive in calm years and are worth everything in a crisis. India's much-criticised Qatari contract is a case study in paying for insurance you hope to waste.

info.name: Natural gas & LNG
info.everyday: Cooking gas cylinders, piped kitchen gas, electricity, and urea fertiliser — which is made from gas
info.india: About half of India's gas is imported as LNG. Expensive gas raises both the power bill and the fertiliser subsidy the government pays.

supplies.share: ~90% of the world's most advanced chips
supplies.rank: Effectively a monopoly at the leading edge
supplies.why_now: Production is normal. The amber is for how much rests on it: the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced chips are made on one seismically active island in a contested strait, using machines only one company makes. New plants elsewhere are being built precisely because this concentration is uncomfortable, and they are years from relieving it.
supplies.what: One company, TSMC, on one island, makes the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced processors. Nothing else in the modern economy is this concentrated in this few buildings. The machines required come from a single Dutch supplier, which narrows it further.

dependents.detail: Design the chips; TSMC is the only firm that can make them at the leading edge
Every advanced AI processor is made here
Electronics assembly and car manufacturing both depend on chips from this island

risks: Military tension in the Taiwan Strait
Earthquakes — Taiwan is seismically active, and a 2024 quake briefly halted production
Drought, since chip fabrication uses enormous quantities of ultra-pure water
Concentration itself: the most advanced capacity sits in a handful of facilities
supplies.if_disrupted: Reputable estimates of a serious disruption run into trillions of dollars of lost output — larger than anything else on this page. Phones, cars, servers, appliances and defence systems are all affected, and replacement capacity takes three to five years to build even with unlimited money.
supplies.india: Car and electronics production, and the cost of nearly every device. India's semiconductor mission exists substantially because of this one concentration.

history.what: A severe drought in 2021 forced Taiwan to truck water to chip plants during the global shortage. In April 2024 a magnitude 7.4 earthquake briefly halted production.
history.why: Chip fabrication needs vast amounts of ultra-pure water and absolute vibration stability. Taiwan has periodic droughts and sits on an active fault.
history.how_long: The 2024 earthquake caused days of disruption; the 2021 drought ran for months.
history.response: Taiwan prioritised water to the chip industry over agriculture — paying farmers to leave fields fallow. TSMC built extensive water recycling. Governments elsewhere accelerated subsidy programmes to build capacity outside Taiwan.
history.lesson: Taiwan chose chips over farming when water ran short, which tells you how the trade-offs work when a single industry is that strategically important. It also shows the risk is not only military — weather and geology can do it too.

info.name: Advanced chips
info.everyday: Phones, cars, appliances, ATMs, UPI itself — a modern car has over a thousand
info.india: India designs a lot of chips and manufactures almost none of the advanced ones yet. The 2021 chip shortage left Indian car buyers waiting months.

supplies.share: Largest LNG exporter in the world
supplies.what: American shale transformed the world's energy balance in about fifteen years, turning a large importer into the largest exporter of LNG. Shale responds far faster than conventional oil — months rather than years — which makes US supply the modern shock absorber alongside Saudi spare capacity.

dependents.detail: Replaced Russian pipeline gas largely with American LNG after 2022
Japan, South Korea and increasingly India

risks: Export permit policy, which shifts with administrations
Hurricanes in the Gulf of Mexico shutting terminals
Freeport-style terminal accidents — a single facility is a meaningful share of exports
supplies.if_disrupted: Global gas prices rise, with Europe most exposed. A US export restriction would be a policy choice rather than an accident, and would reprice gas worldwide.
supplies.india: India has signed long-term US LNG contracts to diversify away from Gulf supply. More American gas means more competition and generally lower prices for Indian buyers.

history.what: An explosion at the Freeport LNG terminal in Texas took about 20% of US export capacity offline. European gas prices rose sharply; US domestic prices fell.
history.why: A single facility handled a large share of exports. The accident split the market in two — gas was suddenly trapped inside the US.
history.how_long: About eight months to return to full service.
history.response: Safety reviews across US terminals; Europe leaned harder on Qatari and Norwegian supply.
history.lesson: One terminal can be a geopolitical event. Export infrastructure is as concentrated a risk as production itself, and is easier to damage.

info.name: Natural gas & LNG
info.everyday: Cooking gas cylinders, piped kitchen gas, electricity, and urea fertiliser — which is made from gas
info.india: About half of India's gas is imported as LNG. Expensive gas raises both the power bill and the fertiliser subsidy the government pays.

supplies.what: The US and Brazil between them are roughly 70% of world soy, and they harvest at opposite times of year, which gives the market two chances a year to go wrong and two chances to be saved.

dependents.detail: The dominant buyer; the trade dispute of 2018 showed how much that matters to both sides

dependents.who: Global feed and edible oil markets
dependents.detail: Soy is the pivot of both

risks: Drought in the Midwest during the critical pod-filling weeks
Trade policy — Chinese tariffs redirected the entire trade flow in 2018
Low water on the Mississippi, which is how most of the crop reaches port
supplies.if_disrupted: Edible oil and animal feed prices rise together, pushing up cooking oil, chicken, eggs and milk at once.
supplies.india: Soy oil is part of India's edible oil import basket and soymeal sets poultry feed costs, so a US drought reaches an Indian kitchen through two separate doors.

history.what: China imposed 25% tariffs on US soybeans in the trade dispute. US exports to China collapsed and Brazilian soy went to a large premium.
history.why: Soybeans were targeted precisely because they were America's largest agricultural export to China and politically concentrated in states that mattered.
history.how_long: About two years, partly resolved by the 2020 trade agreement.
history.response: The US paid farmers roughly $28 billion in compensation. China bought more from Brazil, which permanently accelerated Brazil's rise to dominance.
history.lesson: Trade weapons reshape supply chains permanently. China's switch to Brazilian soy did not reverse when the tariffs eased — once a buyer builds a new relationship, it keeps it.

info.name: Soybeans & soy oil
info.everyday: Cooking oil, and — as animal feed — the real cost behind chicken, eggs and milk
info.india: India imports soy oil as part of its edible oil basket, and soymeal prices feed straight into Indian poultry and dairy costs.

supplies.what: About a third of the US corn crop goes into ethanol for fuel rather than food, which means American energy policy is a food policy for the rest of the world. Most of the rest feeds animals.

dependents.detail: Major importers for feed and food
Corn is the main feed grain worldwide

risks: Midwest drought, the single biggest factor
Ethanol mandates, which divert a third of the crop regardless of food demand
Mississippi river levels — low water has repeatedly disrupted barge shipments to port
supplies.if_disrupted: Feed costs rise globally and meat, eggs and dairy follow a few months later. Corn shortages are experienced as protein inflation.
supplies.india: India grows most of what it needs, but world corn prices set the floor under poultry feed. India's own ethanol programme is now creating the same food-versus-fuel tension domestically.

history.what: The worst US drought since the 1930s cut the corn crop sharply and prices hit records. World food prices rose with them.
history.why: A severe Midwest drought during pollination. The ethanol mandate meant a fixed share of a shrunken crop still had to go to fuel, which worsened the shortage for food and feed use.
history.how_long: About a year.
history.response: Livestock producers petitioned to waive the ethanol mandate; the request was refused. Importers turned to Brazil and Ukraine.
history.lesson: A fixed mandate becomes a multiplier in a shortage. When a third of a crop is legally committed to fuel, a 20% harvest loss becomes a 30% loss for everyone eating it.

info.name: Corn (maize)
info.everyday: Animal feed first, then starch, sweeteners and ethanol — most of it is eaten by livestock, not people
info.india: India grows most of what it uses, but world corn prices set the cost of poultry feed, which is why chicken prices track a crop grown in Iowa.

supplies.share: Largest cotton exporter in the world
supplies.what: The US exports most of what it grows, which makes it the swing supplier to the world's garment manufacturers — and highly exposed to drought in Texas, which produces much of the crop.

dependents.detail: The garment manufacturing centres

risks: Texas drought, which has repeatedly caused farmers to abandon large areas unharvested
Trade restrictions related to sourcing standards
supplies.if_disrupted: Yarn and fabric prices rise, which raises clothing costs worldwide.
supplies.india: Indian cotton growers gain from a US shortfall; Indian textile mills competing with Bangladesh for cheap cotton lose.

history.what: Severe Texas drought caused US farmers to abandon roughly 40% of planted cotton area — the highest abandonment rate on record.
history.why: Extreme drought made harvesting uneconomic. Insured farmers were better off claiming than picking.
history.how_long: One season, with effects into the following year.
history.response: Importers turned to Brazil and Australia, both of which expanded planting.
history.lesson: Crop insurance changes behaviour during a drought: when claiming pays better than harvesting, the supply loss is larger than the weather alone would cause.

info.name: Cotton
info.everyday: Clothing, bedsheets, towels — roughly a quarter of the world's fibre
info.india: India is a top producer and the backbone of its textile industry, which is one of the country's largest employers after agriculture.

supplies.share: ~8-10% of world wheat exports, plus ~45% of sunflower oil
supplies.rank: Among the top wheat exporters; dominant in sunflower oil
supplies.why_now: The war continues and it is being fought partly over export infrastructure. Ukraine ships grain through its own Black Sea corridor, which has worked better than expected, but port and power facilities are struck periodically and farmland remains mined. Output is well below pre- war levels and the labour to work it is not all coming back.
supplies.what: Ukraine's black soil is among the most fertile on earth, and the country feeds a large part of North Africa and the Middle East. Its sunflower oil share is the striking one — close to half the world's supply, which makes it a direct substitute market for palm oil.

dependents.detail: The world's largest wheat importer, and bread subsidies are politically fundamental there
Heavily reliant on Black Sea grain
Buys Ukrainian sunflower oil, which competes with palm in the edible oil basket

risks: War damage to fields, storage, rail and port infrastructure
Black Sea shipping security and insurance availability
Labour shortages and mined farmland, which persist long after fighting stops
supplies.if_disrupted: Wheat and sunflower oil prices rise, and the burden falls on low-income importing countries. The 2022 episode was followed by political unrest in several of them — food price shocks have toppled governments before.
supplies.india: Sunflower oil is part of India's edible oil import basket, so a Ukraine disruption pushes Indian cooking oil prices up alongside palm. India is largely self-sufficient in wheat, so that side is mostly indirect.

history.what: Ukrainian exports were blockaded after the invasion. Wheat hit records and sunflower oil became scarce, with rationing in some European supermarkets.
history.why: Ports were blockaded and mined, and no commercial ship would sail without security guarantees or insurance.
history.how_long: About five months to the first grain deal; the arrangement collapsed in July 2023 and Ukraine then opened its own coastal corridor.
history.response: The UN and Turkey brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative. When that failed, Ukraine ran a corridor hugging NATO-member coastlines, which worked better than expected and restored much of the volume.
history.lesson: Food exports found a way through an active war. Routes are more adaptable than they look — but the adaptation took a year, and a year of expensive bread is a long time if you are poor.

info.name: Wheat
info.everyday: Atta, bread, biscuits, noodles, maida
info.india: India mostly grows its own, but world prices still set the floor under domestic wheat and feed into bread and biscuit costs.

supplies.what: Peru's large mines sit high in the Andes, and the ore travels to port on a small number of roads that pass through local communities. Those communities have repeatedly blockaded the roads over disputes about water, land and the distribution of mining revenue.

dependents.detail: The dominant buyer, and owner of several of the largest mines
Peru and Chile together are roughly a third of world supply

risks: Community road blockades, which stop exports without stopping mining
Political instability — Peru has had repeated changes of president
Water disputes with highland farming communities
supplies.if_disrupted: Combined with any Chilean problem, a Peruvian disruption tightens the copper market quickly, because between them these two countries are roughly a third of world production.
supplies.india: Copper feeds Indian construction, electrical goods and the grid build-out. Higher copper prices raise the cost of electrifying India.

history.what: Protests and road blockades repeatedly halted copper transport from major mines including Las Bambas, at times for weeks.
history.why: Long-running disputes between mining companies and local communities over revenue sharing, land and water, intensified by national political turmoil.
history.how_long: Recurring over two years, with individual blockades lasting days to weeks.
history.response: Negotiated settlements with communities, higher local revenue shares, and in some cases military escort of convoys. Miners began holding larger stockpiles at port.
history.lesson: Supply can be interrupted without any mine closing. The weakest link is often the road, not the resource — and social licence is as real a risk as geology.

info.name: Copper
info.everyday: Every wire in your home, every motor, every charger, the electricity grid itself
info.india: India imports copper concentrate. It is also the metal the whole electrification push runs on, so this is a long-term structural dependence, not a passing one.

supplies.share: Historically dominant; now modest, but a major platinum producer
supplies.rank: ~70% of world platinum and most palladium outside Russia
supplies.what: South Africa's gold mines are the deepest in the world and long past their peak. The live story is platinum group metals, which go into catalytic converters that clean car exhaust — and the mines run on an electricity grid that has been failing for years.

dependents.detail: Every petrol car with a catalytic converter needs these metals
Platinum is central to fuel cells and electrolysers

risks: Load-shedding — scheduled national power cuts that directly reduce mine output
Deep-mine safety incidents and ageing infrastructure
Rail and port bottlenecks at Transnet limiting exports
supplies.if_disrupted: Platinum and palladium prices rise, which raises car manufacturing costs. It also makes catalytic converter theft more profitable — a surprisingly direct consumer effect that has occurred worldwide.
supplies.india: Car manufacturing input costs, and South Africa is a significant source of Indian gold imports. The platinum link is small but real for Indian vehicle exporters meeting emissions standards.

history.what: National electricity shortages forced mines to shut. In 2008 mines closed for five days and platinum spiked; the 2022-23 load-shedding was the worst on record and cut output across the industry.
history.why: Decades of under-investment in power generation, compounded by maintenance failures and, in 2008, by a sudden grid emergency.
history.how_long: 2008 was days; the recent episode ran for years at varying intensity.
history.response: Mines invested in their own solar and battery generation to become independent of the national grid — effectively building private power systems.
history.lesson: Infrastructure decay is a slow supply risk that nobody prices until it bites. Electricity is an input to mining as surely as the ore is.

info.name: Gold
info.everyday: Jewellery, weddings, and the thing Indian households save in when they trust nothing else
info.india: India is the second largest consumer in the world and produces almost none of it. Gold imports are the second biggest item on the import bill after oil.

supplies.what: Thailand is the swing supplier in rice. When India restricts exports, buyers turn here — and Thai prices rise accordingly. It is also a major natural rubber producer, which matters for tyres.

dependents.detail: Major buyers, especially when Indian supply is restricted
Regular large buyers

risks: Drought, particularly during El Niño years
Flooding in the central plains, which has repeatedly destroyed crops
Baht strength making Thai rice uncompetitive
supplies.if_disrupted: With India already the dominant exporter, a Thai problem on top removes the main alternative and the rice price rises sharply. The rice market is thin — a small share of world production is actually traded — so it moves far more than wheat for the same disruption.
supplies.india: Mostly a competitive matter: Thai problems raise Indian rice export earnings. For Indian consumers the effect is negligible.

history.what: Severe floods inundated central Thailand, killing over 800 people and submerging industrial estates as well as farmland.
history.why: An unusually heavy monsoon season met a dense industrial zone built on a flood plain.
history.how_long: Months of disruption; some factories took over a year to restart.
history.response: Large flood defence investment and a government rice-pledging scheme that backfired badly, accumulating enormous unsold stockpiles.
history.lesson: The floods also halted global hard disk drive production — Thailand made a large share of them — and computer prices rose worldwide. A flood in one country became a technology shortage, which is how supply chains actually transmit shocks.

info.name: Rice
info.everyday: The staple on half the world's plates
info.india: India is the largest exporter, so here the risk runs the other way: when India restricts exports to protect its own prices, the shortage lands on buyers in Africa and Asia.

supplies.what: Thailand is the biggest supplier of the one material that heavy tyres cannot do without. Most of it comes from smallholders with a few hectares each, which makes supply responsive to the daily tapping decision of hundreds of thousands of individual farmers.

dependents.detail: The largest buyer, for the world's biggest tyre industry
A major tyre manufacturer and net importer

risks: Leaf fall disease, which has spread through Southeast Asian plantations
Flooding in the southern growing provinces
Low prices causing farmers to stop tapping, which is a decision made daily
supplies.if_disrupted: Tyre costs rise, which raises vehicle prices and road freight costs — and freight is an input to the price of nearly everything.
supplies.india: Indian tyre manufacturers' raw material costs, which flow into the cost of running every truck in the country.

history.what: Rubber prices reached multi-year highs after floods and leaf disease cut Thai and Indonesian output.
history.why: A decade of low prices had discouraged replanting and tapping; disease then hit an already-ageing tree stock, and floods finished the season.
history.how_long: Ongoing; the seven-year maturity of a rubber tree means no quick recovery.
history.response: Tyre makers raised prices and increased synthetic content wherever technically permissible.
history.lesson: The same pattern as cocoa: a long stretch of prices too low to justify investment quietly builds a shortage that arrives years later, looking sudden.

info.name: Natural rubber
info.everyday: Tyres above all — a truck tyre needs natural rubber that synthetic cannot replace — plus gloves, footwear and seals
info.india: India is a major tyre manufacturer and a net importer of rubber. Kerala grows some, nowhere near enough.

supplies.what: Thailand matters in sugar out of proportion to its size because it exports most of what it makes, which makes it the main alternative when India restricts.

dependents.detail: Regional buyers

risks: Drought, particularly during El Niño years
Farmers switching between cane and cassava based on relative prices
supplies.if_disrupted: With Brazil and India dominating, a Thai shortfall removes the swing supply and the world price rises.
supplies.india: A competitor in export markets. Thai problems improve Indian sugar export prospects when India is allowing exports.

history.what: A severe drought cut Thai cane output by roughly a third, and world sugar prices rose.
history.why: One of the worst droughts in decades, worsened by upstream water use and a weak monsoon.
history.how_long: Two seasons.
history.response: Farmers switched area to cassava, which needs less water. Sugar mills operated far below capacity.
history.lesson: When a crop becomes unreliable, farmers switch to something else — and that switch outlasts the drought, permanently shrinking the supply base.

info.name: Sugar
info.everyday: Sweets, soft drinks, biscuits, and — through ethanol — a slice of your petrol
info.india: India is both a huge producer and a swing exporter. Policy here moves the world price, and the world price moves Indian sugar company profits.

supplies.what: Malaysia is the stabiliser in palm oil: smaller than Indonesia but far more predictable, with fewer sudden policy changes. When Indonesia restricts exports, buyers including India turn here first.

dependents.detail: A major buyer and the first alternative when Indonesia restricts
Food manufacturing and oleochemicals

risks: Labour shortages on plantations — a chronic constraint
El Niño reducing yields with a 6-12 month lag
EU deforestation regulation restricting market access
supplies.if_disrupted: With Indonesia already dominant, a Malaysian problem removes the only meaningful alternative and edible oil prices rise sharply across Asia.
supplies.india: Directly: cooking oil prices. Malaysia is India's hedge against Indonesian policy, so problems here remove an important safety margin.

history.what: Pandemic border closures cut off the migrant workers Malaysian plantations depend on. Fruit went unharvested and output fell even though the trees were healthy.
history.why: Plantations rely heavily on migrant labour, mostly from Indonesia and Bangladesh. Closed borders meant no workers, and palm fruit must be harvested within days of ripening.
history.how_long: About two years, easing as borders reopened.
history.response: Recruitment agreements with source countries and mechanisation efforts, which have proved difficult on steep plantation terrain.
history.lesson: A supply chain can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the resource. The trees were fine; the people who pick them could not get there.

info.name: Palm oil
info.everyday: The cheapest cooking oil, plus soap, biscuits, chocolate, instant noodles and cosmetics
info.india: India is the world's biggest buyer of edible oils and imports roughly 60% of what it uses, most of it palm. A palm oil shock reaches an Indian kitchen within weeks.

supplies.share: ~2% of world output, but Africa's largest producer
supplies.rank: Major supplier of light sweet crude
supplies.what: Nigeria is included not for volume but for grade. Its light, low-sulphur crude is exactly what European and Indian refineries are configured for, so it is not easily replaced by heavier Gulf barrels even when the barrel count works out.

dependents.detail: Configured for this specific grade
A long-standing supplier, though displaced somewhat by discounted Russian crude

risks: Oil theft and pipeline sabotage in the Niger Delta, which have at times removed a large share of output
Chronic under-investment in production
Currency and subsidy crises affecting domestic refining
supplies.if_disrupted: Specific refineries struggle even if world oil volume is adequate, because not all crude is interchangeable. This is a quiet point worth understanding: 'enough oil' and 'the right oil' are different questions.
supplies.india: Indian refiners are unusually flexible and can process many grades, which is a genuine competitive advantage and part of why India became a refining export hub.

history.what: Nigerian output fell to multi-decade lows, at times under a million barrels a day against an OPEC quota nearly twice that, largely due to theft.
history.why: Industrial-scale oil theft from pipelines, plus years of under-investment. At one point a large share of the oil entering a major pipeline never arrived.
history.how_long: Years; partial recovery after security contracts were awarded in late 2022.
history.response: Private security contracts to protect pipelines — including with former militants — and the eventual start-up of the Dangote refinery to process crude domestically.
history.lesson: A country can hold a production quota it is physically unable to fill. Official capacity and actual output can diverge for years, which is why OPEC quota announcements often matter less than they appear to.

info.name: Crude oil
info.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
info.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

supplies.rank: Largest producer by a wide margin
supplies.why_now: Mining is running, but two things keep this amber. Sulphuric acid — which the extraction method depends on — has been in short supply, and export routes historically ran through Russia, so shipments now take longer and costlier paths. Meanwhile demand is rising as countries restart nuclear programmes.
supplies.what: Kazakhstan mines more uranium than the next three countries combined, using a low-cost method that dissolves the ore underground rather than digging it out. As countries turn back to nuclear power for clean electricity, this is a dependence that is growing rather than shrinking.

dependents.detail: Building more reactors than anyone and a major buyer
Both depend on imported uranium; the US produces very little of its own
Imports uranium for its civil nuclear programme under international agreements

risks: Landlocked geography — most exports historically travelled through Russia
Political instability, as in the January 2022 unrest
Sulphuric acid shortages, which the extraction method depends on
supplies.if_disrupted: Uranium prices rise and nuclear utilities, which plan fuel years ahead, scramble for alternative supply. Electricity prices follow only slowly, because fuel is a small share of a reactor's cost — but the strategic anxiety is immediate.
supplies.india: India's nuclear expansion plans depend on imported fuel. A quieter dependence than oil, and one that grows as India builds more reactors.

history.what: Violent unrest across Kazakhstan triggered by a fuel price rise led to a state of emergency and an internet shutdown. Uranium prices jumped on supply fears.
history.why: The removal of a price cap on liquefied petroleum gas, used widely as vehicle fuel, roughly doubled prices overnight and set off nationwide protests.
history.how_long: Mining was barely affected; the price spike faded within weeks.
history.response: The government reversed the fuel price rise and a Russian-led security force was deployed briefly.
history.lesson: A fuel subsidy removal set off unrest that threatened nearly half the world's uranium supply. Energy price policy is a political stability question in producing countries, and their instability becomes everyone's supply risk.

info.name: Uranium
info.everyday: Nuclear electricity — about a tenth of the world's power, and rising as countries look for clean baseload
info.india: India imports uranium for its civil reactors under international agreements, and nuclear is central to its clean-power plans.

supplies.rank: Holds most of the world's remaining reserves
supplies.what: This is the most absolute concentration on this entire page, and almost nobody knows about it. Phosphorus is one of three elements plants cannot grow without, it cannot be manufactured or substituted, and the large majority of what is left in the ground is in one country.

dependents.detail: Imports nearly all its phosphatic fertiliser needs; a long-term supply relationship with Morocco's OCP
Its enormous soy and corn crops depend on imported phosphate
Structural importers

risks: Export pricing decisions by a single state-controlled producer
Cadmium content rules in Europe restricting which rock can be sold
Energy costs, since processing rock into usable fertiliser is energy-intensive
Disputes over Western Sahara, where some deposits lie
supplies.if_disrupted: Fertiliser costs rise, and the effect appears a full growing season later as lower yields. It is the slowest-acting item on this page and among the most consequential, because it reduces how much food exists rather than how much it costs to move.
supplies.india: India imports essentially all of it, so this feeds straight into the fertiliser subsidy bill and into farm economics. One of India's least discussed and most complete dependencies.

history.what: Phosphate fertiliser prices roughly tripled as energy costs soared and China restricted its own exports to protect domestic farmers.
history.why: Expensive natural gas raised processing costs, and China — a major exporter — stopped exporting to keep its own farmers supplied, removing a large chunk of world supply at once.
history.how_long: About two years before prices normalised.
history.response: India raised fertiliser subsidies sharply and negotiated long-term supply agreements with Morocco and Saudi Arabia to reduce reliance on Chinese supply.
history.lesson: There is no substitute for phosphorus and no way to make more of it. Of every dependency on this page, this is the one with the fewest available answers — which is precisely why so little attention is paid to it.

info.name: Phosphate rock
info.everyday: The P in NPK fertiliser. There is no substitute — plants need phosphorus and it cannot be manufactured
info.india: India imports nearly all of it. One of the least-known and most absolute dependencies on this page.

supplies.what: Potash is the K in NPK fertiliser — the part that makes crops hardier and raises yields. Saskatchewan holds enormous reserves, and Canada's importance grew sharply when Belarus, previously a top-three exporter, became difficult to buy from.

dependents.detail: Imports 100% of its potash — there are no commercially viable deposits in the country
Major buyers for their large agricultural sectors
Palm oil plantations are heavy potash users

risks: Rail capacity in western Canada, which is the only way the product reaches port
Mine flooding, a recurring hazard in potash mining
Belarus and Russia returning fully to the market, which is a price risk rather than a supply one
supplies.if_disrupted: Fertiliser prices rise and yields fall the following season. Potash is more easily skipped for a year than nitrogen or phosphate, so farmers respond by simply using less — which quietly degrades soil over time.
supplies.india: India's potash dependence is total, which is why Indian negotiators sign multi-year contracts and why the fertiliser subsidy is so exposed to this one market.

history.what: Potash prices roughly tripled after sanctions on Belarus and then on Russia removed roughly 40% of world export supply.
history.why: Belarus was sanctioned over a forced airliner landing, and Lithuania stopped carrying its potash to port — cutting off a landlocked exporter's only route. Russian supply became difficult after the invasion of Ukraine.
history.how_long: About eighteen months.
history.response: Canada expanded output. India signed direct long-term contracts with Canadian and Israeli suppliers and raised subsidies to shield farmers.
history.lesson: A landlocked exporter can be cut off by a neighbour refusing transit, with no sanction on the goods themselves. Transit rights are as much a chokepoint as any strait.

info.name: Potash
info.everyday: The K in NPK fertiliser, which is what makes crops resilient and improves yields
info.india: India imports 100% of its potash. There are no commercially viable deposits in the country at all.

supplies.share: ~45% of world soybean meal and oil exports
supplies.rank: Largest exporter of processed soy products
supplies.why_now: The crop recovered from the 2023 drought, but export taxes and a currency farmers do not trust mean beans sit in silo bags rather than reaching the market. The harvest existing and the harvest being sold are different things here, and policy decides which.
supplies.what: Argentina grows less soy than Brazil but crushes far more of it, exporting the oil and the animal feed rather than the raw bean. That makes it the world's largest supplier of the two things soy is actually used for.

dependents.detail: A major buyer of Argentine soy oil for the edible oil basket
Large buyers of soymeal for animal feed

risks: Recurring drought, which has repeatedly halved the crop
Export taxes, which Argentina uses heavily for government revenue and which farmers respond to by hoarding
Currency controls and multiple exchange rates, which make farmers reluctant to sell
supplies.if_disrupted: Cooking oil and animal feed prices rise together. Argentina's problems are unusually often self-inflicted through tax and currency policy rather than weather, which makes them harder to forecast from satellite images.
supplies.india: Argentine soy oil is a direct component of India's edible oil imports. When Argentina's crop fails or its farmers refuse to sell, Indian cooking oil prices feel it.

history.what: The worst drought in sixty years cut Argentina's soy crop by roughly half, and export taxes plus currency distortions made farmers reluctant to sell what remained.
history.why: Three consecutive La Niña years brought severe drought. Separately, a 33% export tax and an unfavourable official exchange rate gave farmers every reason to store beans rather than sell them.
history.how_long: About two years.
history.response: The government introduced a special 'soy dollar' exchange rate to coax farmers into selling — effectively a temporary devaluation for one crop.
history.lesson: A harvest existing is not the same as a harvest reaching the market. When a government's currency policy makes selling irrational, the supply disappears as surely as if it had never grown.

info.name: Soybeans & soy oil
info.everyday: Cooking oil, and — as animal feed — the real cost behind chicken, eggs and milk
info.india: India imports soy oil as part of its edible oil basket, and soymeal prices feed straight into Indian poultry and dairy costs.

supplies.why_now: Export controls on the most advanced lithography machines remain in force, and licensing for the tier below keeps shifting. Nothing has stopped for buyers outside China; the amber is because a single company in a single country is now an instrument of trade policy, and the rules change.
supplies.what: One Dutch company, ASML, is the only firm on earth that makes the machines required to print the most advanced chips. Each costs upwards of $200 million, contains hundreds of thousands of parts, and ships in multiple aircraft. Taiwan makes the chips; the Netherlands makes the only machines that can make them.

dependents.detail: Every leading-edge chip plant in the world runs on these machines
Restricted from buying the most advanced models, which is the single most consequential export control in force today
Relevant to the semiconductor fabrication plants India is building

risks: Export control policy, which has made these machines an instrument of geopolitics
Extreme supply chain complexity — a single specialist component supplier can hold up production
Retaliation affecting the company's large service business in China
supplies.if_disrupted: No immediate consumer price effect, and an enormous long-term one: without these machines no new leading-edge chip capacity can be built anywhere. It is the bottleneck behind the bottleneck.
supplies.india: India's semiconductor ambitions depend on access to this equipment. India is building mature-node plants first, which need less restricted machines — a sensible sequencing given this constraint.

history.what: The Netherlands, under US pressure, restricted exports of advanced lithography machines to China. China responded by stockpiling older machines and restricting gallium, germanium and graphite exports.
history.why: An attempt to slow Chinese progress at the leading edge of chipmaking, using the one point in the supply chain where a Western ally holds a monopoly.
history.how_long: Ongoing.
history.response: China accelerated domestic equipment development and bought every unrestricted machine available. Western firms lost significant service revenue.
history.lesson: Everyone looks for chokepoints in raw materials. The most powerful one in the modern economy is a machine made by one company in one country — and both sides of a dispute will reach for whatever monopoly they happen to hold.

info.name: Chipmaking machines
info.everyday: Nothing you can buy — but no advanced chip exists without these machines, so everything with a chip depends on them
info.india: Relevant to India's semiconductor plans: you cannot build a leading-edge fab without machines only a handful of firms make.

supplies.share: ~25% of world bauxite output, largest reserves
supplies.why_now: Bauxite keeps loading, but Guinea has been pressing miners to build refining capacity locally — following Indonesia's nickel playbook — and has suspended some export permits to make the point. Politics there moves the aluminium price without a single tonne being lost.
supplies.what: Bauxite is the rock aluminium comes from, and Guinea has more of it than anywhere else. It is also one of the poorest countries in the world, with a history of coups, which is an uncomfortable combination for anyone depending on it.

dependents.detail: Buys the majority of Guinea's bauxite to feed the world's largest aluminium smelting industry
Through China, essentially everyone

risks: Political instability — a coup in 2021 sent aluminium prices up immediately
Rainy season disruption to mining and barge loading
Export policy pushing for domestic refining, following Indonesia's example with nickel
supplies.if_disrupted: Aluminium prices rise, which raises the cost of packaging, construction, vehicles and power cables. The effect reaches consumers through drinks cans and window frames rather than anything obviously strategic.
supplies.india: India has its own bauxite and smelting, so Indian producers benefit from higher world prices while Indian manufacturers pay more.

history.what: A military coup in Guinea sent aluminium to a ten-year high within days, even though bauxite shipments were never actually interrupted.
history.why: The market priced the risk, not the event. With one country supplying a quarter of the world's bauxite, the possibility of disruption was enough.
history.how_long: Prices eased within weeks once the junta confirmed mining would continue.
history.response: The military government moved quickly to reassure mining companies, since the revenue was essential to it.
history.lesson: Markets price the risk of disruption, not just disruption itself. And resource revenue usually protects mining from political upheaval — the new government needs the money as much as the old one did.

info.name: Aluminium & bauxite
info.everyday: Cans, foil, window frames, aircraft, electricity cables, and increasingly car bodies
info.india: India has bauxite and significant smelting capacity, so it is a competitor here — but smelting is enormously power-hungry, which ties it to coal prices.

supplies.rank: Largest producer for over a century
supplies.what: Silver is no longer mainly a precious metal: more than half of demand is now industrial, and solar panels are the fastest-growing use. Most silver is also a by-product of mining lead, zinc and copper, so its supply does not respond to the silver price.

dependents.detail: Every panel contains silver paste; this demand has grown enormously
One of the largest importers in the world, for jewellery and a fast-growing solar industry
Silver is the best electrical conductor there is

risks: Mining law changes and permitting disputes, which have tightened in recent years
Labour disputes at the large mines
By-product economics — silver output depends on decisions made about other metals
supplies.if_disrupted: Silver prices rise, raising solar panel costs at exactly the moment the world is trying to install more of them. This is a quiet constraint on the energy transition that gets far less attention than lithium.
supplies.india: India's silver import bill is large and growing, driven by both wedding demand and solar manufacturing. It is a smaller version of the gold problem, with an industrial engine behind it.

history.what: Silver moved to multi-year highs as solar demand pushed the market into a sustained deficit for several consecutive years.
history.why: Solar installation grew far faster than forecast while mine supply was flat, because silver output is decided by lead and zinc mining economics rather than by the silver price.
history.how_long: Ongoing structural deficit.
history.response: Panel manufacturers worked to reduce silver loading per panel, cutting it substantially — the same engineering response seen with cobalt in batteries.
history.lesson: When a metal is a by-product, high prices cannot summon more of it. The only lever is using less per unit, which is why thrifting matters more than exploration for silver, cobalt and palladium alike.

info.name: Silver
info.everyday: Jewellery and investment, but more than half of it is industrial now — solar panels above all
info.india: India is one of the largest silver importers in the world, for both jewellery and a fast-growing solar industry.

supplies.rank: Largest robusta producer; second largest coffee producer overall
supplies.why_now: Robusta is still recovering from the drought that drove record prices. Growing area has shrunk because farmers switched land to durian, which paid better, and trees planted now take three to four years to bear. Supply is tight until that replanting matures.
supplies.what: Brazil dominates arabica, the smoother bean. Vietnam dominates robusta, the stronger and cheaper one that goes into instant coffee and espresso blends. Between them they set the price of nearly every cup in the world.

dependents.detail: Robusta is the base of almost all instant coffee
The main export markets
Also a robusta grower, so Vietnamese shortfalls lift Indian export prices

risks: Drought in the Central Highlands growing region
Farmers switching to durian and pepper, which have at times been far more profitable
Ageing trees and slow replanting
supplies.if_disrupted: Instant coffee and blended coffee prices rise, and because robusta is the cheap bean there is nothing cheaper to switch to — buyers must move up to arabica, which pushes that market up too.
supplies.india: Indian coffee growers benefit. Indian instant coffee consumers pay more.

history.what: Robusta prices hit record highs after drought in Vietnam's Central Highlands, and arabica rose alongside it as buyers switched up.
history.why: An El Niño drought hit during the critical flowering period, and years of farmers switching land to more profitable durian had already shrunk the growing area.
history.how_long: Over a year.
history.response: Roasters reformulated blends and absorbed costs where they could; Vietnamese farmers expanded planting in response to the price.
history.lesson: The cheap substitute failing is worse than the expensive one failing, because there is nowhere further down to go. When robusta rises, the whole coffee market has to move with it.

info.name: Coffee
info.everyday: Your cup, and the price on every café menu
info.india: India grows and exports coffee, so a Brazilian frost is good news for Indian growers and bad news for Indian drinkers.

supplies.rank: Third producer and a growing exporter
supplies.what: Vietnam is the third pillar of a supply base concentrated in three neighbouring Southeast Asian countries. Together Thailand, Indonesia and Vietnam are about two-thirds of the world's natural rubber.

dependents.detail: The dominant buyer for its tyre industry
A net importer for its own large tyre industry

risks: Typhoons in the central growing regions
Land competition from more profitable crops
EU deforestation regulation affecting market access
supplies.if_disrupted: With supply concentrated in three adjacent countries sharing a climate, a regional weather event can hit all three at once — which is the real risk here, rather than any single country failing.
supplies.india: Tyre manufacturing costs, and therefore road freight costs.

history.what: A leaf disease outbreak spread across Southeast Asian rubber plantations, cutting yields in Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam simultaneously.
history.why: Pestalotiopsis leaf fall disease spread through plantations with little genetic diversity — most commercial rubber trees are closely related clones.
history.how_long: Several seasons; the disease remains present.
history.response: Fungicide programmes, which are expensive for smallholders, and slow replanting with more resistant varieties.
history.lesson: Genetic uniformity is a supply chain risk. When every tree in a region is near-identical, one disease can take them all — which is as true of crops as of computer systems.

info.name: Natural rubber
info.everyday: Tyres above all — a truck tyre needs natural rubber that synthetic cannot replace — plus gloves, footwear and seals
info.india: India is a major tyre manufacturer and a net importer of rubber. Kerala grows some, nowhere near enough.

supplies.share: ~8% of production but ~25% of world tea exports
supplies.what: Kenya exports almost everything it grows, which makes it far more important to the world tea trade than its production share suggests. Its tea is grown at high altitude by hundreds of thousands of smallholders and goes largely into the blends sold in Britain, Pakistan and Egypt.

dependents.detail: The largest buyer of Kenyan tea; tea is a significant item in its import bill
Major buyers for blended black tea

risks: Drought and erratic rainfall in the highlands
Frost at high altitude, which can damage bushes outright
Currency shortages in buying countries — Pakistan has at times been unable to pay
supplies.if_disrupted: Black tea prices rise, felt most in Pakistan, Egypt and the UK. A regional rather than global effect, but severe for the countries involved.
supplies.india: A direct competitor in export markets, so Kenyan shortfalls raise Indian tea export prices. Little effect on Indian domestic prices.

history.what: The worst drought in forty years hit the Horn of Africa, cutting Kenyan tea output. At the same time Pakistan, its largest buyer, faced a dollar shortage and struggled to pay for imports.
history.why: Four consecutive failed rainy seasons, combined with a balance of payments crisis in the main export market.
history.how_long: About two years.
history.response: Kenya sought new buyers; Pakistan's government asked citizens to drink less tea to save foreign exchange — a widely mocked request that reflected a genuine crisis.
history.lesson: A supply chain can break at the buyer's end. Kenya had tea it could not sell because its customer had no dollars — a reminder that demand failing is as disruptive as supply failing.

info.name: Tea
info.everyday: The most-drunk prepared beverage on earth after water
info.india: India is both a top-two producer and a huge consumer. Domestic prices are set mostly at home, so this is an export-earnings story rather than an inflation one.

routes.name: Strait of Hormuz
routes.headline: A fifth of the world's oil leaves through a gap 33 km wide
routes.volume: About 20 million barrels of oil a day, plus a fifth of all the LNG traded at sea
routes.why_it_matters: Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar, the UAE and Iran all ship through the same narrow channel, and at its tightest the usable shipping lanes are about 3 km wide in each direction. There is no way around it for most of this oil: the pipelines that bypass it can carry only a fraction.
routes.if_blocked: This is the single most consequential thing that could happen to world prices. Crude would not rise by a few percent — past scares alone have moved it 10-20%, and an actual sustained closure is generally reckoned to put oil well above $150. Petrol, diesel, bus fares, airline tickets, plastics and fertiliser all follow within weeks. Gas-importing countries would be bidding against each other for cargoes that no longer exist.
routes.india: India sources a large share of its crude from Gulf producers that must use Hormuz. A closure would hit the rupee, the inflation rate and the fiscal deficit simultaneously — the three things that decide whether the RBI can cut rates. Of everything on this page, this is the one that would change an Indian household budget fastest.
routes.alternatives: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline to the Red Sea and the UAE's Fujairah pipeline together bypass only about a quarter of normal flows, and the Red Sea exit has had its own problems. For practical purposes there is no alternative at scale.
watch: Tanker insurance (war-risk premium) rates for the Gulf — they move before the news does
Whether tankers are switching off their tracking transponders
Naval escort announcements by the US, China or India

history.what: The 'Tanker War' during the Iran-Iraq conflict: both sides attacked each other's oil shipping, and over 450 vessels were hit.
history.why: A land war between two oil exporters extended to each other's main source of revenue — the tankers.
history.how_long: Four years, ending with the wider ceasefire in 1988.
history.response: The US reflagged Kuwaiti tankers under its own flag and escorted convoys through the Gulf — a naval operation to keep a commercial route open.
history.lesson: The strait has never actually been closed, even during a war fought largely over it. Closing it hurts the countries that use it most, including the one doing the closing. Threats are common; closure is not.

history.what: Tankers were attacked near the strait and a drone was shot down; oil jumped around 4% in a day and war-risk insurance for the region multiplied several times over.
history.why: Escalation between the US and Iran after sanctions were tightened.
history.how_long: Weeks of elevated risk; no closure.
history.response: An international maritime escort mission; buyers quietly diversified toward US and African crude.
history.lesson: Most of the economic damage of a chokepoint scare arrives through insurance and freight costs long before any ship is actually stopped.

carries_detail.name: Crude oil
carries_detail.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
carries_detail.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

carries_detail.name: Natural gas & LNG
carries_detail.everyday: Cooking gas cylinders, piped kitchen gas, electricity, and urea fertiliser — which is made from gas
carries_detail.india: About half of India's gas is imported as LNG. Expensive gas raises both the power bill and the fertiliser subsidy the government pays.

routes.name: Suez Canal
routes.headline: The shortcut between Asia and Europe — or an extra 10 days around Africa
routes.volume: Normally about 12-15% of world trade and roughly 30% of all container traffic
routes.why_it_matters: Without it, a ship from Mumbai to Rotterdam goes around the Cape of Good Hope: roughly 10-14 extra days and a great deal more fuel. That extra time does not just cost money, it removes ships from the world fleet — the same vessels can make fewer trips a year, so freight rates rise everywhere even for routes nowhere near Egypt.
routes.if_blocked: Container freight rates spike within days and stay high while the diversion lasts. Goods arrive late, factories waiting on parts slow down, and the cost shows up in imported goods a quarter or two later. Egypt also loses billions in transit fees, which becomes its own currency problem.
routes.india: India's trade with Europe runs through here. Longer voyages raise landed costs for engineering goods, textiles and chemicals exporters, and squeeze margins for importers of European machinery.
routes.alternatives: The Cape of Good Hope works and is entirely safe — it is simply much longer. There is no fast alternative.
watch: Container freight rate indices on the Asia-Europe route
Suez Canal Authority transit numbers, published monthly
Red Sea security, since a safe canal with a dangerous approach is no use

history.what: The container ship Ever Given wedged across the canal and blocked it completely for six days. Over 350 ships queued.
history.why: High winds and a sandstorm in a narrow single-lane section, with questions raised about speed and piloting.
history.how_long: Six days to refloat; several weeks to clear the backlog.
history.response: Dredging and tugs refloated it at spring high tide. Egypt afterwards widened and deepened the southern section and added a second lane over part of the route.
history.lesson: One ship, six days, and roughly $9 billion a day of trade held up. Efficiency and fragility are the same thing seen from different sides — a route with no slack has no room for an accident.

history.what: The canal was closed for eight years after the Six-Day War, with 15 ships trapped inside for the entire period.
history.why: War between Egypt and Israel; the canal became a front line.
history.how_long: Eight years.
history.response: World shipping simply adapted — and in adapting, built the supertanker. Ships got far larger because the long route around Africa made size economic.
history.lesson: Long disruptions do not just raise prices, they permanently change the system. The supertanker exists because the Suez closed.

carries_detail.name: Crude oil
carries_detail.everyday: Petrol and diesel, bus and auto fares, plastics, paint, fertiliser, and the delivery cost of nearly everything else
carries_detail.india: India buys about 88% of its crude from abroad. It is the single largest item on the import bill, so the oil price sets the rupee, the inflation rate and the government's budget maths at once.

carries_detail.name: Natural gas & LNG
carries_detail.everyday: Cooking gas cylinders, piped kitchen gas, electricity, and urea fertiliser — which is made from gas
carries_detail.india: About half of India's gas is imported as LNG. Expensive gas raises both the power bill and the fertiliser subsidy the government pays.

carries_detail.name: Container shipping
carries_detail.everyday: The freight cost buried inside the price of every imported thing you own
carries_detail.india: Roughly 95% of India's trade by volume moves by sea. Freight rates are a tax on everything, paid invisibly.

routes.name: Bab el-Mandeb & the Red Sea
routes.why_now: Shipping through the Red Sea is still running well below normal. Attacks on vessels from 2023 pushed most container lines onto the route around Africa, and although the threat has eased, war-risk insurance for the passage stayed expensive and the big carriers have been slow to come back — a routing decision, once made, is costly to reverse. This clears when the major lines publicly resume Suez transits and insurance prices fall back toward normal.
routes.headline: The southern door to the Suez — and the one that has actually been shut
routes.volume: Normally around 9 million barrels of oil a day and most Asia-Europe container traffic
routes.why_it_matters: The Suez Canal is only useful if ships can reach it. Bab el-Mandeb is the 20-mile gap at the bottom of the Red Sea that every Suez-bound ship from Asia must pass. Shut this and the canal above it is stranded, which is exactly what happened from late 2023.
routes.if_blocked: Ships divert around Africa. In the 2024 episode, Suez traffic fell by more than half, Asia-Europe container rates rose several times over, and delivery times stretched by two weeks. Insurance for the Red Sea became prohibitively expensive, which did more to reroute shipping than the attacks themselves.
routes.india: Indian exporters to Europe faced sharply higher freight and longer payment cycles, which hurts smaller firms most because they finance the gap. India also had to extend naval patrols into the Arabian Sea.
routes.alternatives: Around the Cape of Good Hope — safe, and about 10-14 days longer.

history.what: Houthi forces in Yemen attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Most major container lines stopped using the route and sailed around Africa instead.
history.why: The attacks were declared to be in response to the war in Gaza — a political conflict expressing itself through a trade route.
history.how_long: More than a year of significantly reduced traffic; recovery has been gradual and incomplete.
history.response: Multinational naval escort operations; shipping lines rerouted and raised rates; some manufacturers moved to holding larger inventories again.
history.lesson: A chokepoint does not need to be physically blocked to stop working. It only needs to become uninsurable. Risk, not blockade, is what reroutes ships.

routes.name: Strait of Malacca
routes.headline: Asia's oil lifeline, and the narrowest point is under 3 km wide
routes.volume: About 23-25 million barrels of oil a day — more than Hormuz — plus a quarter of all traded goods
routes.why_it_matters: Almost all the oil going from the Gulf to China, Japan and South Korea passes through here. It is long, shallow in places, heavily trafficked and narrows to about 2.8 km at the Phillips Channel near Singapore.
routes.if_blocked: East Asia's energy supply would be in immediate difficulty. China has called this its "Malacca dilemma" for two decades and has spent heavily on pipelines through Myanmar and Central Asia, and on the Belt and Road, very largely to reduce this one dependence.
routes.india: India sits beside the western approach, which is a strategic asset: the Andaman and Nicobar Islands overlook it. For Indian trade with East Asia it is the main artery, and for Indian policy it is quiet leverage.
routes.alternatives: The Sunda and Lombok straits through Indonesia can take the traffic but add days and cannot handle the deepest-draft vessels well.

history.what: Piracy in the strait became serious enough that insurers briefly designated it a war-risk zone in 2005.
history.why: Weak coastal enforcement, high traffic, and ideal geography for small fast boats.
history.how_long: Several years of elevated risk, falling sharply after 2006.
history.response: Coordinated patrols by Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, plus joint air surveillance — the 'Eyes in the Sky' programme.
history.lesson: Chokepoint security is usually fixed by the neighbouring states cooperating, not by distant navies. It worked here and has been the model since.

routes.name: Panama Canal
routes.headline: A canal that runs on rainwater — and can run short of it
routes.volume: About 5% of world seaborne trade, and a much larger share of US east coast trade with Asia
routes.why_it_matters: Unlike Suez, which is a sea-level ditch, Panama lifts ships 26 metres over the isthmus using locks. Every transit spends roughly 200 million litres of fresh water from Gatun Lake, which is filled by rain. A drought is therefore a capacity problem, which is a genuinely unusual way for a trade route to fail.
routes.if_blocked: Transits get rationed and slots are auctioned, so only the highest-value cargo pays to cross. Everything else goes around South America or across the US by rail. US consumer goods, LNG exports and grain shipments are hit hardest.
routes.india: Indirect but real. Rerouted ships tighten the world fleet, which raises freight rates everywhere including on Indian routes, and it lifts the delivered cost of US LNG that India buys.
routes.alternatives: Around Cape Horn, or US land bridge by rail, or — for Asia-to-US-east-coast traffic — the Suez instead, which simply moves the dependence to a different chokepoint.

history.what: A severe drought cut daily transits from about 36 ships to as few as 22. Some operators paid millions at auction to jump the queue.
history.why: El Niño conditions produced the driest year on record for the canal watershed. The canal competes for the same water that supplies drinking water to Panama City.
history.how_long: About a year, easing as rains returned in mid-2024.
history.response: Transit rationing and slot auctions; a long-term plan to dam the Rio Indio for extra water storage, which requires relocating communities and remains contested.
history.lesson: Climate is now a trade-route risk, not just an agricultural one. A route can fail without anyone attacking it.

routes.name: Turkish Straits & the Black Sea
routes.why_now: Grain is moving out of Ukraine again through a corridor hugging the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts, but it runs without a formal agreement and depends on the war staying away from the ports. Strikes on Odesa's infrastructure have repeatedly interrupted loadings. This stays amber while the corridor rests on nothing more than restraint.
routes.headline: The world's bread basket has one narrow way out
routes.volume: Normally around a quarter to a third of world wheat exports, plus sunflower oil and Russian crude
routes.why_it_matters: Ukraine and Russia together supply a very large share of the world's wheat, barley, sunflower oil and fertiliser, and nearly all of it leaves through the Bosphorus — a strait that runs through the middle of Istanbul and is about 700 metres wide at its narrowest.
routes.if_blocked: Wheat prices rise globally within days, and the pain lands hardest on low-income countries in North Africa and the Middle East that import most of their bread grain. Fertiliser follows, which damages the NEXT harvest everywhere — the second-order effect is larger and slower than the first.
routes.india: India grows most of its own wheat, so the direct hit is modest. The indirect hit is fertiliser: India imports heavily, and the 2022 spike forced a sharp increase in the subsidy bill. A hungry world also pressures India to export grain it may want to keep.
routes.alternatives: Rail and barge through Europe, and Danube river ports. Both work and both carry a fraction of the volume at much higher cost.

history.what: Russia's invasion of Ukraine halted Black Sea grain exports. Wheat prices hit record highs and fertiliser roughly tripled.
history.why: Ports were blockaded and mined; shipping would not sail without security guarantees or insurance.
history.how_long: Roughly five months to the first grain deal, then an on-off arrangement that collapsed in July 2023.
history.response: The UN and Turkey brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which moved about 33 million tonnes before Russia withdrew. Ukraine then opened its own corridor hugging the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts, which worked better than expected.
history.lesson: Food is not just a commodity, it is a lever. And the fertiliser effect matters more than the grain effect — the first hits this year's bread, the second hits next year's harvest everywhere.

routes.name: Cape of Good Hope
routes.headline: Not a chokepoint — the escape route when the others fail
routes.volume: Varies enormously: whatever Suez and Panama cannot take
routes.why_it_matters: It is wide, deep and safe, with no canal authority, no locks and no tolls. Its only cost is time — 10 to 14 extra days between Asia and Europe. That makes it the pressure valve for the whole system, and the reason a Suez or Red Sea closure raises prices rather than stopping trade entirely.
routes.if_blocked: It effectively cannot be. The practical risk is the opposite one: when everyone uses it at once, the extra sailing days absorb so much of the world fleet that freight rates rise globally even though no route is shut.
routes.india: This is the route Indian exporters fell back on during the Red Sea disruption. It works — it just costs more and takes longer, which is hardest on small exporters financing the gap.

history.what: Traffic around the Cape rose sharply as ships abandoned the Red Sea. South African ports struggled to service the extra vessels.
history.why: Diversion from Bab el-Mandeb.
history.how_long: Ongoing through the Red Sea disruption.
history.response: Shipping lines added vessels to maintain weekly schedules, which absorbed spare capacity worldwide and pushed up rates on unrelated routes.
history.lesson: A safety valve has a cost, and the cost is paid by everyone — including shippers on routes that were never disrupted.

routes.name: Taiwan Strait
routes.why_now: Nothing is physically interrupted. The amber is for concentration rather than an event: the overwhelming majority of the world's advanced chips cross this strait, military exercises around the island have become routine, and replacement capacity elsewhere is years from mattering. This is a standing exposure, not a developing incident.
routes.headline: Where the world's advanced chips are made, and shipped
routes.volume: Roughly a fifth of all container traffic passes through, but the real cargo is irreplaceable
routes.why_it_matters: This is the only entry on this page where the risk is not really about shipping. Taiwan makes the overwhelming majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, and those factories cannot be replicated quickly at any price. The strait is the physical expression of a dependence no alternative route can solve.
routes.if_blocked: Estimates of the cost of a serious disruption run into trillions of dollars — larger than any other single item on this page. Cars, phones, servers, appliances and defence equipment would all be affected, and replacement capacity takes years, not months, to build.
routes.india: India's electronics assembly and car industries depend on these chips, and the 2021 shortage already showed what that feels like — months-long waits for new cars. It is also the central reason behind India's semiconductor fabrication push.
routes.alternatives: For shipping, around the east of Taiwan. For the chips themselves, there is no alternative at the leading edge — which is the entire point. New fabrication plants in the US, Japan and India are being built precisely to change that, over a decade.

history.what: A global semiconductor shortage halted car production lines worldwide. Carmakers lost millions of units of output.
history.why: Carmakers cancelled chip orders early in the pandemic expecting a slump; demand instead surged, and by the time they tried to reorder, the capacity had been sold to consumer electronics. Chip plants take years to build, so the gap could not be closed.
history.how_long: About two and a half years.
history.response: Governments responded with subsidy programmes — the US CHIPS Act, the EU Chips Act, and India's own semiconductor mission — to put capacity closer to home. Carmakers abandoned just-in-time inventory for chips and began buying direct from manufacturers.
history.lesson: The shortage was not caused by a disaster. It was caused by a forecast being wrong in an industry with multi-year lead times. Concentration plus long lead times is dangerous even with no villain in the story.
